item.content:encoded:
This could be the final MLB game for quite some time as the Milwaukee Brewers have a chance to sweep the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series on Tuesday night.
Milwaukee scored eight runs with two outs in the fifth inning in Game 3 last night, putting up 10 runs without a home run in the 10-1 victory.
There have now been just two home runs through three games in this series, both of which came in Game 2.
Nevertheless, I have a home run pick for each team in World Series Game 4 tonight.
Here’s a complete breakdown of these home run props for Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Best MLB Home Run Prop Bet Picks for Tuesday, Oct. 27.
- Yandy Diaz to Hit a Home Run (+800)
- William Contreras to Hit a Home Run (+540)
Yandy Diaz to Hit a Home Run (+800)
There weren’t any home runs in Game 3, but Yandy Diaz came pretty darn close. His 413-foot double with an exit velocity of 111.4 miles per hour would’ve been a home run in 22 of 30 ballparks, according to Baseball Savant. He also had a single with an exit velocity of 115.5 miles per hour.
Diaz had 22 home runs in the regular season and went deep twice in the ALCS. I’ll take this long +800 price given the power he has and how well he’s seeing the ball right now.
William Contreras to Hit a Home Run (+540)
I am going down with the ship.
After hitting 18 home runs in the regular season, Contreras has gone deep three times this postseason. The last one came in NLCS Game 2, the start of a six-game hitting streak for the slugger.
Contreras is now 18-for-43 (.419) with three home runs and a double in 11 postseason games. He’s racked up eight RBI and six runs as well.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are favored to take Game 3 on Monday, but their chances of capturing their first ever World Series title have dwindled.
The Rays jumped out to a 4-0 first inning lead in Game 2, but through the game’s final eight innings the offense sputtered and the defense, nor pitching from ace Drew Rasmussen, was as sharp as needed to hold down the Brewers, who earned a 5-4 victory.
The pair of one-run victories in Milwaukee have put the Brewers in prime position for their first title. Nearly 81% of MLB teams that have generated a 2-0 series lead in the World Series have gone on to win the title.
To disrupt that statistic, the Rays will need to find a way to win Game 3. Kalshi traders make their odds 53% as of Monday morning.
For informational purposes only. Not trading advice. See full disclaimer below. Kalshi is the Official Prediction Market Partner of the Atlanta Braves, Los Angeles Dodgers, San Francisco Giants, San Diego Padres, and Boston Red Sox.
World Series Game 3 Odds: Rays favored in home ballpark
Right-handed pitcher Freddy Peralta had a rough start to his 2026 campaign when pitching for the New York Mets. But after being dealt to the Rays, he’s unlocked a former version of himself, one the Milwaukee Brewers know quite well. Peralta pitched for the Brewers for eight seasons before being traded to the Mets in the offseason. The Mets dealt him to the Rays at the trade deadline.
As such, now he’ll need to square off against his former team in World Series Game 3, looking to extend an incredible stretch of pitching which saw him earn ALCS MVP honors.
Across three starts and one relief appearance this postseason, Peralta has thrown 16.2 innings and allowed just two earned runs, good for a 1.08 ERA.
But the Brewers represent a level up offensively. Milwaukee finished the regular season tied for first in wRC+ against right-handed starters and led the league in on-base percentage and batting average against the handedness.
On the other hand, the Rays will draw left-handed starter Robert Gasser. Like the rest of the Milwaukee staff, Gasser has been fantastic this postseason, throwing nine innings over the course of two starts and allowing just one earned run.
Southpaws have been a challenge for the Rays this season, with the team ranking 26th against lefties in terms of wRC+ during the regular season. Even if they are able to get through Gasser, the Milwaukee bullpen features lefties JoJo Romero, DL Hall, and Aaron Ashby, and has been nearly unhittable, collectively posting a 1.23 ERA in nearly 51 innings this postseason.
Nevertheless, Kalshi traders make the Rays, who posted a 55-26 record at home during the regular season, slight favorites at 53% in Game 3.
The Rays overcame a 2-1 deficit in the ALCS, but they face a stiffer test against baseball’s top team in the World Series.
Regardless of the Game 3 winner, Game 4 will take place on Tuesday in Tampa Bay. In early trading, Kalshi traders make the Brewers slight favorites on the road in that game, pricing them at 50%.
Should a Game 5 be necessary, it will take place on Wednesday in Tampa Bay. If Games 6 or 7 are required, those will take place back in Milwaukee after a travel day.
Through two games, Brewers catcher William Contreras is the favorite for World Series MVP, according to Kalshi traders.
Contreras is trading around 38% to earn the award while outfielder Jackson Chourio is trading at 17% and left-handed reliever Aaron Ashby is priced at 15%.
In their two home victories, Contreras has notched four hits in eight at-bats and driven in two runs for Milwaukee. Plus, he’s thrown out multiple runners attempting to steal and helped manage a pitching staff through two tense one-run victories.
Chourio has posted similar stats, netting four hits in his nine at-bats, while stealing two bases and cutting down a runner at the plate with an outfield assist during Game 2.
Though less heralded coming into the series, Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby has been dominant all postseason, pitching 15.2 innings without allowing a single run. That includes more than three innings of World Series play in which he’s only allowed one hit.
Down 2-0, the highest priced Ray player is Junior Caminero, who is trading around 6% to win the award.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Guardians Make Decision on Trading Steven Kwan
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen

item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Guardians, whether they’ve intended to or not, have dealt with Steven Kwan trade rumors for more than a year.
They’ve now reached an offseason, to add to the mix, where Kwan will seem more likely than ever to be traded.
Kwan is a standout ballplayer, both a quality leadoff hitter and a Gold Glove defender in left field. Most teams in MLB would be interested in him if he ended up on the block.
Add in the fact that this is the last season of Kwan’s current contract coming up, and that he’s due for a raise in salary arbitration, and it really aligns with the timeline when the Guardians often trade their best players (that aren’t named Jose Ramirez).
Kwan isn’t new to the rumor mill, though. He was floated as a trade candidate as early as the 2025 trade deadline. It didn’t happen then, or last offseason, or at this year’s trade deadline.
Could the Guardians hold Kwan now and still trade him at the 2027 deadline? Sure. But the most likely time Cleveland would trade Kwan, if it’s going to happen, would be this winter — lockout permitting.
The Guardians recently made clear how they feel as an organization about this possibility, and it’s worth noting even while recognizing that things could change in a hurry in the NFL.
Guardians Make Steven Kwan Trade Decision
The Guardians have made it clear that they don’t intend to trade Kwan.
“As we sit here today, we’re expecting Steven Kwan to be a big part of a contending team next year,” Guardians president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti shared recently, via Cleveland.com’s Paul Hoynes.
That’s obviously what a front office leader is going to say at this point in the timeline. It wouldn’t benefit Antonetti to share different thoughts publicly.
Still, it’s at least a positive sign for any Guardians fans who want to keep Kwan around going forward.
Guardians Conundrum
The Guardians often reach a point like this. They’re unlikely to be the team to give Kwan his next long-term contract unless he offers a steep sale price for his deal.
But this is also a team that just played six games in the ALCS. Can they really trade away one of their best players?
It’s a question that big-market teams don’t have to answer, but Cleveland doesn’t fit that descriptor. This is a franchise that has to contemplate moves like trading Kwan before he leaves a year later in free agency.
The Guardians are saying they won’t do it, and maybe that’s true. But the rumors will persist anyway, because it would fit the bill for Cleveland, and because many fans are intrigued by the idea of having Kwan on their team instead.

item.content:encoded:
Jonathan Aranda has become a pivotal player for the Tampa Bay Rays.
By the end of the regular season, he had the second-most homers (22) in the franchise, behind Junior Caminero (42).
Before he enters the 2026 World Series, let’s learn five fast facts about his wife, who has watched him grow in his career.
1. They Got Married in 2025
On Oct. 24, 2025, the pair got married.
This means their first anniversary will take place during the World Series this year — a rare way to celebrate.
2. She Threw a Ceremonial First Pitch
On May 16, 2026, Milka threw the first pitch for Tampa Bay’s clash against the Miami Marlins at Tropicana Field.
Unfortunately, the Rays ended up facing a 10-5 loss to the Marlins that day, but they did end up winning the three-game series.
3. They Have a Daughter
Jonathan and Milka have a 2-year-old daughter named Regina.
Following her birth, he discussed how being a father has changed him.
“It’s definitely changed a little bit,” he said, per Adam Berry of MLB.com. “Now it’s a little easier because now I’m doing everything for her and our family.”
During that conversation, he also joked about having newfound “dad strength.”
4. Milka Is From Mexico
Not only is Jonathan from Mexico, but so is his wife.
Jonathan became the first Mexican-born first baseman, and they now proudly instill their culture in their daughter.
5. She Was With Jonathan Long Before He Exploded in the Big Leagues
Their early relationship was kept fairly quiet, but she has had the opportunity to watch him grow into the elite hitter he is today.
During the regular season, he slashed .274/.358/.434with a .792 OPS and a career-high 22 homers through 155 games.
Their marriage remains relatively private.
Where Do the Rays Stand Ahead of Game 1?
ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – SEPTEMBER 2: Jonathan Aranda #8 of the Tampa Bay Rays at bat in the bottom of the first inning against the New York Mets at Tropicana Field on September 2, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images)
Tampa Bay enters the World Series as an underdog.
The Brewers appear to hold a slight edge over the Rays, but this isn’t shocking considering they led the majors 103-59 overall during the regular season.
Tampa Bay dominated during the ALDS and the ALCS, leading up to the moment they’ve been waiting for — a run in the Fall Classic.
KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI – JUNE 24: Manager Kevin Cash #16 of the Tampa Bay Rays talks with reporters prior to a game against the Kansas City Royals at Kauffman Stadium on June 24, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Ed Zurga/Getty Images)
There’s always a chance they could upset Milwaukee, but doing so will be on easy feat.

item.title: [mlb.com] Our experts make their World Series predictions
item.dc:creator: Max Ralph
item.description: The Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were a franchise record, navigated a tight NL Division Series against the Padres before clobbering the two-time reigning champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series sweep. item.content:encoded:
The Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were a franchise record, navigated a tight NL Division Series against the Padres before clobbering the two-time reigning champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series sweep. It’s just the second World Series appearance in their history and their first since 1982.
Meanwhile, the Rays swept the division rival Yankees in the ALDS before handling the Guardians in six games in the ALCS. They’re back in the Fall Classic for the third time and the first since 2020.
Both teams do a little bit of everything right on the diamond, making for what should be a thoroughly exciting World Series. Here’s how our group of MLB.com experts see it playing out.
Rays vs. Brewers
The pick: Brewers (43 of 51 votes, 84.3%)
Why they’ll win
Any time you take down the back-to-back reigning champs, and do so in a sweep, it’s going to make noise. But really, this is nothing new for the 2026 Brewers. They owned the best regular-season record with a roster that just gets the job done across the board.
The Brewers can play small ball, but they can slug when it matters most, too. In fact, Milwaukee has been more homer-dependent in October than it was all year. But the club can still work a deep count and get on base in many ways. Just ask Jake Bauers.
On the mound, it’s no secret that the bullpen is the Brewers’ strength. One of the best groups in the regular season is only doing more of the same in October, with a 1.33 ERA in eight games. Lefty Aaron Ashby is leading the charge during a historically good run. And then there’s that Jacob Misiorowski guy, who has been good enough in the playoffs but could unleash a new, dominant level in the World Series.
What they’re saying
“There's something about this Brewers club. Maintaining the league's best record all summer and barely giving an inch so far in the postseason, they're looking pretty unstoppable with the right mix of clutch hits, key performers and an absolutely lockdown bullpen. It might finally be the Crew's moment in the spotlight.” -- Adrian Garro, editorial producer
“The Brewers have been knocking on this door for years and are firing on all cylinders following their impressive sweep of the Dodgers. They are smart and hard-nosed enough not to let the long layoff affect them negatively.” -- Andrew Werle, supervising editor, content operations
“Walking off Mason Miller. Sweeping the 2-time defending champion Dodgers. These Brewers may just be a team of destiny, with their final obstacle being the American League's top-seeded Rays.” -- Kyle Boris, supervisor, media operations
The dissenting view
The Brewers have been dominant, but so have the Rays. They have a clear edge in starting pitching, with Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez firing on all cylinders. The Tampa Bay bullpen, while not as overpowering as the Brewers’, is still strong and has lockdown closer Bryan Baker waiting in the wings.
The key for the Rays likely lies in their lineup, where Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda appear to be heating up at the right time. Much like Milwaukee, the Rays will put together quality at-bats, get on base and then cause havoc on the basepaths. Perhaps no one is more adept at doing so than Chandler Simpson.
“The Rays' ‘small ball’ doesn't slump, and they've been pressing all of the right pitching buttons.” -- Jonathan Mayo, national reporter, prospects
“With their Big 3 of Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero breaking out at the end of the ALCS -- plus a slight edge over the Crew in starting pitching -- I believe the Rays are going to steal Game 1 vs. The Miz and ride that to a World Series title. Third time is a charm.” -- Brian McGrath, supervising editor, content operations
Series predictions
Brewers (6 games): 23 votes
Brewers (7 games): 14 votes
Brewers (5 games): 5 votes
Rays (7 games): 4 votes
Rays (6 games): 3 votes
Rays (5 games): 1 vote
Brewers (4 games): 1 vote
There may have been an overwhelming majority of our group predicting the Brewers to win the World Series, but that doesn’t do justice to how close these two teams seem to be. This will: 44 of 51 voters see the series going at least six games.
Who will be named World Series MVP?
Jackson Chourio (MIL): 16 votes
William Contreras (MIL): 13 votes
Jacob Misiorowski (MIL): 6 votes
Yandy Díaz (TB): 5 votes
Brice Turang (MIL): 5 votes
Aaron Ashby (MIL): 1 vote
Jake Bauers (MIL): 1 vote
Junior Caminero (TB): 1 vote
Trevor Megill (MIL): 1 vote
Drew Rasmussen (TB): 1 vote
Chandler Simpson (TB): 1 vote
It’s not hard to see why Chourio was our experts’ favorite to take home the World Series Most Valuable Player Award. Still just 22 years old, Chourio already leads Brewers franchise history with six career playoff home runs. He’s already shown he can rise to the occasion this year with a walk-off single against Mason Miller in the NLDS and a massive homer against Blake Snell in the NLCS. But Chourio’s overall production this October has been quiet (6-for-35). It might just be a matter of time before he breaks out.
“Chourio is due to break out in the World Series. While he hasn't done much in the playoffs so far, his two homers were impactful -- a go-ahead shot and a game-tying blast. He's ready to let it rip.” -- Kelsie Heneghan, senior coordinator, social media editorial, MiLB
“He's a legend in the making. This is the start of his Hall of Fame case.” -- Will Leitch, senior columnist
Who will be on the mound when the series ends … and what happens?
Trevor Megill (MIL), final out: 24 votes
Aaron Ashby (MIL), final out: 10 votes
Bryan Baker (TB), final out: 6 votes
Jacob Misiorowski (MIL), final out: 6 votes
Bryan Baker (TB), walked off: 3 votes
Drew Rasmussen (TB), final out: 1 vote
Ian Seymour (TB), final out: 1 vote
Megill has been lights-out as the Brewers’ closer, so it’s easy to envision him shutting things down at American Family Field in Game 6 or 7. But don’t be surprised if it’s Ashby continuing his fireman role -- or The Miz coming in for a clutch relief appearance.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Oct 2026, 04:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Benny Sieu)
MILWAUKEE -- The Milwaukee Brewers will be looking for hard-throwing Jacob Misiorowski to regain his dominant regular-season form against the visiting Tampa Bay Rays on Friday in the opening game of the World Series.
Misiorowski, who often tops 100 mph with his fastball, will be opposed by veteran right-hander Nick Martinez in a matchup of teams that have not won the World Series. It is the first meeting of two teams without a World Series title since the Philadelphia Phillies topped the Kansas City Royals in six games in 1980.
Milwaukee, which won a franchise-record 103 games during the regular season, advanced with a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, while the Rays ousted the Cleveland Guardians in six games in the American League Championship Series.
The Brewers' only other World Series appearance was in 1982 when they were in the American League. The charismatic 'Harvey's Wallbangers' lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals in the decisive seventh game.
The Rays will be making their third World Series appearance. They lost to Philadelphia in five games in 2008 and in six games to the Dodgers in 2020.
Misiorowski, considered the favorite for the NL Cy Young Award, was 16-5 with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. The latter two stats were best in the majors.
But the 24-year-old right-hander did not make it through five innings in either postseason start, although the Brewers rallied to win both games. They topped the San Diego Padres 3-2 in Game 1 of the National League Division Series and the Dodgers 2-1 in the NLCS opener.
'I feel good. I feel like the first one might have been a little under what I expected, but the second one was pretty much right where I wanted to be,' Misiorowski said.
Misiorowski worked out of trouble in his postseason starts, allowing three runs on nine hits in 8 1/3 innings with 11 strikeouts and four walks.
'He hasn't been as crisp,' Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said. 'I don't think people are up there thinking it's going to be 104 (mph), and I think they're elated if it's anything less than that. They're obviously looking at an area. They're trying to exploit everything. He's exposed, like all these guys get at some point.'
At the back end, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed six runs over 40 2/3 innings for a 1.33 ERA in the postseason. Closer Trevor Megill has four saves after collecting 30 in the regular season.
Milwaukee was last in the NL in home runs (154) during the regular season but leads all teams in the postseason with 10 homers in eight games. The Rays have hit seven in nine games.
Catcher William Contreras batted .367 with three homers and five RBIs over the Brewers' first two series. Outfielder Jackson Chourio hit .171, but he had two homers and a team-high seven RBIs.
Jake Bauers, who reached the majors with the Rays in 2018, was named the NLCS Most Valuable Player after hitting .286 with one homer and six RBIs against the Dodgers. Bauers set career highs with 26 homers and 86 RBIs during the regular season.
The 36-year-old Martinez pitched in the postseason with San Diego in 2022 and the Cincinnati Reds last season, but he will be making his World Series debut Friday. Ace Drew Rasmussen will start Game 2 with an extra day's rest, with former Brewers ace Freddy Peralta to follow in Game 3.
'It's exciting,' Martinez said Thursday. 'I think as a team, as a staff, we're confident in whoever we call up for the mound. It fell on me, and my job is just to rack up as many outs as we can and keep us in this ballgame.'
Martinez picked up the win in Game 4 of the ALCS when the Rays evened the series with a 7-3 victory at Cleveland. He allowed one run on two hits in 5 1/3 innings.
'He was pitching in pretty cold weather in Cleveland,' said Rays manager Kevin Cash, who was also at the helm for the 2020 World Series. 'Made some adjustments, he got the strike throwing where he wanted, the cutter gone, and the changeup. I don't even know, somebody told me he changed his grip in between innings, between the first and second. I'm glad I didn't know that in the moment.'
Martinez also started Game 3 in the Rays' ALDS sweep of the New York Yankees. He gave up two runs in 3 2/3 innings in an eventual 4-3 Tampa Bay victory.
Martinez is 0-1 with a 4.44 ERA in 12 regular-season games (seven starts) against Milwaukee. He has a 2.93 ERA in eight games at American Family Field.
Rays closer Bryan Baker, who tied for the MLB lead with 41 saves, has five saves in five postseason chances, pitching in seven of the nine games.
Third baseman Junior Caminero, whose 42 homers were second in the AL, has just one hit in 33 at-bats in the postseason.
--Jim Hoehn, Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to a most fantastically interesting World Series, in which focusing on the size of the markets involved completely misses the forest for the trees. It’s a No. 1-vs.-No. 1 matchup, just the sixth time in the past 30 years that’s happened. It’s a pair of fanbases who have never won before, which marks the first time since 1980 (Royals vs. Phillies) that’s happened, and thus only the second time in more than a century, since the previous time had been 1920.
It’s a matchup of teams that have more than a few connections. Note that Tampa Bay’s top two starters, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, each came up with Milwaukee, and were teammates on the 2020-21 Brewers. Note, also, that NLCS MVP Jake Bauers made his debut with Tampa Bay back in 2018, and that Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold spent nine years in the Tampa Bay front office before moving to Wisconsin.
It's more than just that. Depending on how you view your baseball aesthetics, it's a delightfully throwback sort of on-field style. It’s not that these teams eschew analytical thinking -- exactly the opposite, really -- but no team struck out less than the Rays, each team finished in the top five in steals and the bottom 10 in homers, and the bunt hits leaderboard goes “Tampa Bay first, Milwaukee second.”
Throw in a pair of excellent defenses, and you know what you’re going to get here, which is excellent baseball played by a pair of teams that actually look a whole lot like one another. We know what else we're going to get, too: an incredibly interesting series. Which side has the edge?
Catcher
William Contreras, over the past five years, has a pretty solid argument to make as being the best all-around catcher in the National League. While his bat over the last two seasons (110 OPS+) isn’t quite what it was at his peak from 2022-24 (129 OPS+), it’s reliably solid, and then of course he’s been fantastic in eight playoff games, posting a 1.157 OPS with three homers. It’s hard to overstate how important the midseason acquisition of Liam Hicks (129 OPS+ in 41 games for Tampa Bay) was, really helping to lengthen a top-heavy lineup, though he hasn’t done much with the bat in the playoffs. Given relatively similar defensive value, we’ll give a small edge based on track record.
Advantage: Brewers
First base
It's a tale of two winding paths here, as Jonathan Aranda finally had his breakout last season, a decade after he signed as an amateur free agent with Tampa Bay, and of course Jake Bauers' long road to get to this point has been well-chronicled. Bauers has the offensive edge both in terms of power and getting on base, and neither are terribly strong defensive players, so given the mild 2026 regular-season advantage and also the superior performance in October, it’s hard not to choose Bauers on this. Great stories, both.
Advantage: Brewers
Second base
Brice Turang is the best all-around second baseman in the game, pairing excellent defense with a more recently found power stroke, popping 21 homers and driving in 100. The Rays have certainly found some ways to get value out of their second-base duo of Richie Palacios and Ben Williamson, but it’s a relatively below-average spot for Tampa Bay and, either way, we’re comparing to Milwaukee’s best-in-class superstar. This one is probably the biggest mismatch of any pairing on the list.
Advantage: Brewers
Shortstop
Here’s how you know how well-regarded Taylor Walls is on defense: The Rays continue to play him every day despite a near-total lack of offense from the position, as he’s posted all of a .381 OPS this month, and even that was juiced a little by the inexplicable three walks that Cleveland issued him in ALCS Game 6. It’s not just a small-sample thing, either, as Walls has been a routinely ineffective hitter for the entirety of his career.
There’s no doubt that Milwaukee’s Cooper Pratt is a stronger offensive force, though that’s been more good than great, with a league-average line as a rookie and a mostly singles-based approach in the playoffs. While he’s expected to be a quality shortstop as his career progresses, a number of important miscues in the postseason tilt this one to the more surehanded Walls.
Advantage: Rays
Third base
If there’s some argument that this series features more depth than true superstars, then that case falls apart a little at third, where Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero posted his second consecutive 40-plus homer season on his way to, most likely, some high placement on AL MVP ballots. It’s true that prior to his ALCS Game 6 homer, his bat had been relatively quiet in October, but we’re also talking about all of eight games against some of the best pitching the sport has to offer. (The average fastball he’s seen? 96.8 mph.) There’s an obvious speed-and-defense edge for Milwaukee in David Hamilton and Joey Ortiz, but not quite so much that you’d take either or both over Caminero, or that it’s really close at all.
Advantage: Rays
Left field
This is actually the most fun comparison, because who do you like more, the 22-year-old power-and-defense superstar in Jackson Chourio -- the only player in history to have three 20-20 seasons through age-22 -- or the 25-year-old elite speed-and-contact guy in Chandler Simpson, who improved his defense to the point that both were named Gold Glove finalists last week? It’s yet another reminder that there’s more than one way to provide value, and certainly both teams are very pleased with their situations here. It’s hard, though, not to default to Chourio, who might already be a top-20 position player in the sport. If both can run and field, and only one has any power, then the advantage writes itself.
Advantage: Brewers
Center field
In Garrett Mitchell and Jonny DeLuca, you have two very strong defensive center fielders, though you’d probably give the slight edge here to DeLuca. (Cedric Mullins also carries a good glove, though this spot has belonged to DeLuca all month.) The question about their bats is what shape of production you prefer, in that Mitchell struck out considerably more than DeLuca, but he also had an on-base percentage 54 points higher, thanks in large part to a walk rate three times as high. While we’re not weighing postseason performance too much here, it’s worth noting that Mitchell has had some huge hits, while DeLuca mostly has not. This is about as razor-thin as we’ll see here, but even if Mitchell’s glove isn’t as good, it’s still good, and he gets on base. Edge, Milwaukee. A small one, anyway.
Advantage: Brewers
Right field
For everything that Sal Frelick has done for the Brewers over his four seasons with the team -- and he has done quite a bit -- this was not a terribly strong season for him, posting a career-worst 70 OPS+, and he’s managed only three singles and a few walks in the playoffs. That’s not to say that he can’t help the team win in other ways, because he can and does, but Tampa Bay’s Victor Mesa Jr. has been one of the team’s breakout stars, putting up not only a 127 OPS+ but also some truly elite defensive metrics, in just half a season. You’re already familiar, anyway, with his absolute cannon of a throwing arm. Mesa Jr. wasn’t on the Opening Day roster and didn’t even join the Rays for good until late May. He might just be one of the most important players in the World Series, though.
Advantage: Rays
Designated hitter
It would be hard to find two players who mean more to their respective teams than veterans Yandy Díaz (in his eighth season with Tampa Bay) and recently appointed Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich (in his ninth season as a Brewer). Neither plays the field much anymore, nor is either at or near their peak of offensive performance these days. But Díaz far outperformed Yelich during the regular season (124 OPS+ to 91 OPS+, where again, 100 is average), and that’s held true in the postseason, too, where Yelich has been held out of certain games against tough lefties in favor of Andrew Vaughn. At DH, literally the only thing that matters is “dangerous bat,” and that’s Díaz still, after all these years.
Advantage: Rays
Starting pitchers
If we’re talking about each team’s top three starters, which represent the bulk of a postseason rotation, then it’s Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and Robert Gasser for Milwaukee, and Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez for Tampa Bay. Those six pitchers, so far in the playoffs, have combined for a 1.87 ERA. They’re not that good, obviously, with every underlying metric saying that the strikeout rate has been just average, and that they’ve been bailed out to some extent by excellent defense and relief pitching.
Still: When Misiorowski -- the presumptive NL Cy Young winner, the most dominant per-batter pitcher of the moment -- has the highest postseason ERA of these six, you know how strong each team is here. You really can’t look at full-season stats, either, because it goes without saying that the Tampa Bay version of Peralta is a very different pitcher than New York version we saw prior to the Trade Deadline. Misiorowski is the best of the six, but is he that much better than Rasmussen right now, himself an ace? Maybe not.
These are two strengths, but we like Tampa Bay ever so slightly more for one reason: depth. No Milwaukee starter, not even the top ones, has managed to get past five innings in the playoffs so far, which puts a lot of pressure on the bullpens. (There’s a particularly interesting angle here if Tampa Bay’s high-contact, flat-swing hitters can foul off enough Misiorowski pitches to wear him out, as has already happened to him this month.) If you look past the top three, you’d probably take Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax and Ian Seymour to get outs a little more than Milwaukee’s Shane Drohan and Dustin May.
They’re both good, obviously. They’re World Series starting rotations. We’d give the ever-so-slight edge to Tampa Bay in a best of seven.
Advantage: Rays
Relief pitchers
If Milwaukee’s starters have been more good than great this month, then their relievers have more than picked up the slack, as you’ve almost certainly heard the note that in 40 2/3 postseason innings, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed all of six earned runs. While most of the focus there lands on Aaron Ashby or closer Trevor Megill, realize that JoJo Romero has a 47% strikeout rate this month, and that Abner Uribe, Antonio Senzatela, Megill and Ashby are all averaging more than 98 mph on their heaters this month. In fact, it is the second-hardest-throwing bullpen of the pitch tracking era (since 2008) -- at 98 mph even -- and the hardest that doesn’t include Mason Miller.
It makes, then, for an ironic matchup against a Tampa Bay bullpen that is A) also very good but B) does not throw hard, comparatively, at just 93.2 mph. (That goes down slightly, if you don't include Peralta’s impressive appearance in ALCS Game 4.) Much depends on the status of Bryan Baker, their All-Star closer, who was used so heavily against Cleveland that his fastball, which averaged 96.3 mph during the regular season, sunk below 93 mph in ALCS Game 6.
He was still good, of course. All the Rays are. It’s just hard not to go with Milwaukee, given their superior depth and full rest.
Advantage: Brewers
Prediction
It should be clear by now that this is an incredibly tightly matched series between two mirror-image teams, the best in their respective leagues, and you could as easily claim “rust or rest” for Milwaukee after their layoff, no matter which narrative you’d like to go with. Milwaukee has the biggest-name pitcher in Misiorowski; Tampa Bay has clearly the biggest star hitter in Caminero; and both sides play strong defense and win in ways that aren’t just waiting for the homer.
We like that Milwaukee has the home-field advantage, and the bullpen edge, and also that their lineup just seems a little deeper; in the second half of the season, no team -- not the Dodgers, not the Cubs, not anyone -- got more production from the No. 6 through 9 spots in their lineup than Milwaukee. That’s in part because of the middle infield, where the Brewers were third best, while Tampa Bay was third weakest. There’s at least some question about what shape Baker will be in, though three days of rest before the World Series ought to help.
It won’t be a cakewalk, because there’s too much talent and similarity on both sides for that. But every small edge matters, and Milwaukee has enough of them that we expect the second World Series title in city history, and the first for the Brewers franchise. Get ready to slide, Bernie.
Brewers in seven.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 World Series is going to make history. Either the Tampa Bay Rays or Milwaukee Brewers are about to claim their first championship.
So, that's what's at stake. But what should everyone expect?
According to FanDuel, the Brewers are the favorite (-172) and the Rays are the underdog (+148). Yet this is ultimately a 103-win team against a 98-win team, and both clubs play a very similar style of baseball.
It's therefore worth getting in depth with the specifics of this matchup before making any predictions. Who are the key players? What are the key matchups? What are the X-factors that will determine the series?
Let's see what we can see, and then we'll present picks for the winner of the World Series and for the World Series MVP.
World Series Schedule
1 of 6
All Games on Fox
Game 1 (Friday, October 23): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 2 (Saturday, October 24): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 3 (Monday, October 26): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 4 (Tuesday, October 27): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 5 (Wednesday, October 28)*: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 6 (Friday, October 30)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 7 (Saturday, October 31)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
*If necessary
Key Players for the Rays
2 of 6
3B Junior Caminero
Caminero has been the driving force in the Rays' lineup over the last two seasons, slamming over 40 home runs and racking up over 100 RBI in each. Yet he went cool with a season-low .772 OPS in September, and he initially struggled to snap out of it once the postseason began.
That changed in the last three games of the ALCS. The 23-year-old had hits in all three, including a home run in the clincher that he soaked in as much as possible (and then some). Is he back? It sure seems like he's back.
DH Yandy Díaz
Even if he's not as big of a power threat as Caminero, Díaz rarely fails to have a good at-bat or to hit the ball on a line. He's hit an even .300 across the last four seasons, and he led the AL in hits this year.
The 35-year-old was not the MVP of the ALCS, but he could have been. He torched the Cleveland Guardians for a 1.061 OPS and six extra-base hits, culminating in the two-run homer that iced Game 6.
RHP Drew Rasmussen
Even if he didn't get a ton of hype, Rasmussen was a ball-knower's ace in the regular season between 2022 and 2026. He posted a sub-3.00 ERA annually, and he even led the AL in WHIP this season.
Now the secret is out. The 31-year-old's three starts in the playoffs have yielded just three earned runs in 21.0 innings, with 23 strikeouts and only three walks. His changeup has been especially lethal, holding hitters to three hits in 24 at-bats.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Peralta was with the Brewers this time last year, and his journey since then has taken him to lows with the New York Mets and now highs again with the Rays. He's coming into the World Series hot off being named the ALCS MVP.
The 30-year-old doesn't offer a complicated scouting report. He's throwing his fastball about 70 percent of the time in October, daring hitters to beat him on his best pitch. They haven't, going just 8-for-39 against it so far.
RHP Bryan Baker
Baker blew his third save of the year back on May 13. He hasn't blown one since in 53 turns on the mound, along the way allowing just five earned runs in 52.0 innings.
The 31-year-old's velocity has declined throughout the year, but that has yet to translate into any kind of advantage for hitters. It could be because he uses his fastball and changeup in roughly equal tandem, using both to hold hitters to one hit in 21 at-bats thus far in October.
Key Players for the Brewers
3 of 6
LF Jackson Chourio
The Brewers signed Chourio to an $84 million contract before he had played even one game in the majors. It has paid off in the form of three straight 20-20 seasons, and all before he's turned even 23 years old.
On paper, his .171 batting average and .553 OPS say he's not having a good postseason. Yet even if the Brewers would like more consistency, they'll take the clutch gene that has delivered seven RBI, including two that snatched victory from the jaws of defeat.
1B Jake Bauers
There were 137 players who took at least 500 plate appearances this season, and only 12 of them had a better OPS+ than Bauers. Not bad for a 31-year-old who had an 84 OPS+ for his career coming into the season.
Bauers has become a menace of another sort in the playoffs. Even if he only has one multi-hit game, he's shown tremendous patience in racking up a .441 OBP and driving in six runs. He had multiple at-bats that dug the Los Angeles Dodgers' grave as he was winning MVP honors for the NLCS.
C William Contreras
Contreras has regressed a little as a regular-season performer, but you'd never know from how he's hit this postseason. He's hit safely in six of eight games, with three home runs and five RBI.
Also, don't overlook his mastery of the ABS. He challenged a league-high 185 calls from behind the plate this season, and he won 80 of them. He's kept it up in the playoffs, going 8-for-12 and winning some truly game-changing challenges.
RHP Jacob Misiorowski
After making 30 starts and pitching to a 1.80 ERA and a 5.7 K/BB ratio, Misiorowski is going to win the NL Cy Young Award. As soon as he hit 104.8 mph on his first pitch of the playoffs, he seemed ready to tap into still another gear for October.
Except, he hasn't made it past the fifth inning in either of his two assignments, consisting of nine hits and four walks in 8.1 total innings. He clearly isn't gassed, but he'll need to be better to maximize Milwaukee's chances in the World Series.
LHP Aaron Ashby
Milwaukee's entire bullpen has been incredible in the playoffs, handling 40.2 innings and allowing just six earned runs. Trevor Megill and Abner Uribe deserve their flowers, too.
Yet Ashby has simply been on another level, thus far posting 12.1 shutout innings and allowing just four hits and three walks. The next hitter who gets a knock off his curveball, changeup or slider will be the first.
Matchups That Will Define the World Series
4 of 6
Junior Caminero's Bat Speed vs. the Brewers' Velocity
What makes Caminero so dangerous? For one thing, nobody whips the bat through the zone like he does. His average swing this season was 79.5 mph, the highest of any qualified hitter.
In the World Series, though, he'll be up against a Brewers pitching staff that is averaging 98.3 mph on the fastball. That's almost a full mile per hour faster than the hardest-throwing staff of the 2025 playoffs.
Chandler Simpson's Speed vs. the Brewers' Defenders
Simpson is basically a free 90 feet in human form. He had 11 more infield hits than anyone else this season. He also stole 46 bases, and took 21 more bases on wild pitches, passed balls and the like. It all makes him a rare weapon.
The Brewers, though, could be up to stopping him. Their infield was among the very best this season with a total output of +7 Outs Above Average. More to the point, William Contreras was second in the league in caught-stealings.
Jacob Misiorowski vs. the Rays' High-Contact Offense
Misiorowski's contact rate during the regular season was a mere 65.5 percent, easily the best in baseball. Yet he hasn't been nearly as successful at avoiding contact in the postseason, where his rate has jumped to 77.4 percent.
If the San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Dodgers could do that, the Rays should be able to as well. They led MLB with an 81.8 contact percentage during the regular season, and it has only gone down to 77.2 in the postseason.
The Brewers' Lefty Bats vs. the Rays' Righty-Heavy Pitching
It isn't just Jake Bauers. Milwaukee's left-handed hitters as a collective have a 122 wRC+ in the playoffs, and that's despite facing some darn good left-handed pitching. In the NLCS alone, they faced a pair of two-time Cy Young Award winners in Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell.
The Rays aren't nearly as synonymous with left-handed pitching, indeed carrying only three for the ALCS against Cleveland. And one of them (Ian Seymour) isn't looking so hot after carrying a heavy workload in the regular season.
X-Factors That Will Define the World Series
5 of 6
Home Cooking
The best home record in MLB during the regular season? Well, it was a tie at 55-26… between the Rays and Brewers, naturally.
Neither club has fumbled its home-field advantage in the postseason. The Brewers are 4-0 at American Family Field. The Rays are 4-1 at Tropicana Field. So on paper, both teams can claim to have an advantage on their home turf.
That said, it's the Brewers who truly stand to find out. If this series goes the distance, they'll have the honor of hosting the finale in Milwaukee on October 31.
The Three True Outcomes
For the uninitiated, the three true outcomes are strikeouts, walks and home runs. Neither the Rays nor the Brewers was necessarily synonymous with the concept during the regular season, specifically in the sense that they both ranked in the bottom 10 of the league in home runs.
They have since gone on wildly different paths in October. The Brewers' percentage of three true outcomes when on offense is at 47 percent. For the Rays, it's only 31 percent.
Both paths have ultimately arrived in the same spot, but this may be where we find out which one wins the day. Can the Brewers keep winning by racking up walks and homers? Or, will the Rays avoid enough strikeouts to gain the inside track?
Speed and Defense
Regardless of what happens in the TTO department, neither of these teams should be expected to give much away, while both should be expected to take as much as they can get.
In other words, they're both good at fielding the ball and running the bases. The Rays and Brewers each ranked in the top six for defensive efficiency this season. They were both top-five in stolen bases, and separated by just two steals in the end.
In these respects, the World Series should reward baseball purists for their attention. The result could come down to fine margins—a ball just out of reach or a tag applied just in time.
Predicting the Outcome and World Series MVP
6 of 6
For the World Series: Brewers in 6
Regarding my credentials, I had the Brewers sweeping the Dodgers in the NLCS before it happened. So, I've been right at least once in my life.
Yet whereas the Dodgers looked old, slow and generally out of sorts while trying to keep pace with Milwaukee, the Rays are cut from the same cloth as a ballclub. They're younger and more athletic, and committed to playing smart, clean baseball that emphasizes the little things to add up to one big haymaker.
One area where Milwaukee should have an edge is on offense. The Brewers have as many as five hitters you really have to worry about. The Rays really only have three, in Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda.
The Brewers' bullpen stands out as another advantage, even if they'll need more from their starters to avoid their relievers getting overexposed in a longer series. It, too, is deeper than what the Rays have to offer. And let's be real that Milwaukee relievers are simply on a heater right now.
So, congratulations in advance to the Brewers. If anything is worth a 57-year wait, it's a World Series championship.
For World Series MVP: William Contreras
This pick is partially about deferring to a hot hand. The Brewers have gotten contributions from all their hitters in the postseason, but Contreras has been a constant the whole way through. You just can't fake a 1.157 OPS.
Between his ABS challenges and his ability to control the running game, Contreras' defense also stands to be a huge factor in the World Series. He could also be a not-so-secret weapon when Freddy Peralta pitches for the Rays. If anyone knows him, it's the guy who caught him 81 times between 2023 and 2025.

item.title: [MLB.com] Rays-Brewers World Series Game 1 FAQ (Fri., 8 ET on FOX)
item.dc:creator: Adam Berry; Adam McCalvy
item.description: They are among the five current franchises -- with the Mariners, Padres and Rockies -- which have never won the World Series. item.content:encoded:
They are among the five current franchises -- with the Mariners, Padres and Rockies -- which have never won the World Series. But that will change after a clash between the two teams that finished the regular season with the best record in each league. The Brewers won a franchise-record 103 games. The Rays won 98.
One of them will win four more.
“The World Series is about to be [between] two exceptional baseball teams,” Rays president of baseball operations Erik Neander said amid the sprays of champagne and pouring beer in the Tropicana Field clubhouse late Monday night. “It's going to be a blast to watch.”
When is the game and how can I watch it?
Game 1 is Friday at 8 p.m. ET and airs nationally on FOX and FOX Deportes with streaming on FOX One.
All series are available in the US on MLB.TV with authentication to a participating Pay TV provider. Games also are available live internationally, although not in Canada. Sportsnet is MLB's exclusive English language broadcaster in Canada for every postseason game, while TVA Sports will be covering the entire AL postseason and the World Series in French and Broadcaster RDS will cover the entire NL postseason in French.
Who are the starting pitchers?
What better way for the World Series to start than with Rasmussen facing the team that drafted him and dealt him to the Rays five years ago? The Rays obviously didn’t announce their rotation immediately after clinching a spot in the Fall Classic, but their ace will be on four days’ rest and ready to pitch Game 1 of the World Series, as he handled Game 1 of the ALDS and Game 1 of the ALCS. Tampa Bay has won 14 of Rasmussen’s last 15 starts, and the club should be able to roll out ALCS MVP Freddy Peralta -- another former Brewer -- on normal rest in Game 2 before turning to fully rested and ready options like Nick Martinez and Griffin Jax.
Misiorowski’s first pitch of NLDS Game 1 against the Padres was 104.8 mph, the fastest postseason pitch in the pitch-tracking era, which dates back to 2008. But it hasn’t been smooth sailing since then. The Padres made him work, fouling off an incredible 30 pitches in the first four innings to knock Misiorowski out of the game by the fifth at 88 pitches. Then the Dodgers battled him just as tough in Game 1 of the NLCS, seeing 94 Misiorowski pitches in 4 1/3 hard-fought innings in which he limited the damage to one run. Half of their swings -- 21 of 42 -- produced a foul ball.
“Miz, say what you want, you didn't see 105 [mph], whatever, but whenever he got in a jam, he got better,” manager Pat Murphy said that night after the Brewers won the game. “His innings are up to almost 190 this year. That's way over, way over what he's ever done. The kid's bound to be a little bit tired, you know what I mean? You can't expect him to understand what this is all about going this far and having to pitch this much this year with the pressure he's had on him.”
The good news is Misiorowski will be rested. Because the Brewers finished off the Dodgers in four games, he will have gone 11 full days off between pitching against an opponent in a different uniform.
What are the starting lineups?
Rays: Misiorowski isn’t exactly an easy matchup for anyone, but it would make sense for the Rays to use a relatively standard lineup leaning toward left-handed hitters against the Brewers’ flame-throwing ace.
Brewers: The lineup the Brewers used against right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2 produced the second postseason game in franchise history in which five different players tallied multiple hits. Against right-hander Tyler Glasnow in NLCS Game 4, they came back from four runs down to finish a sweep. So, with the Rays likely to start Rasmussen in World Series Game 1, why not roll with the same batting order?
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Rays: The Rays leaned heavily on their starters in the ALDS and ALCS, with Peralta, Jax and Ian Seymour making at least one appearance out of the bullpen. Seymour became a regular left-handed presence in relief, albeit with shaky results in ALCS Game 6. Closer Bryan Baker has finished each of the Rays’ seven postseason wins, working seven scoreless innings so far. Left-hander Cam Booser has clearly established himself as the top left-handed setup man in front of Baker, while Tyler Wells and Kevin Kelly will get the biggest outs against right-handed hitters.
Brewers: Brewers relievers are 7-1 with a 1.33 ERA (six earned runs in 40 2/3 innings this postseason, accounting for every decision in the eight team games so far. That comes after they led MLB with 48 wins and led the NL with a 3.40 ERA in the regular season. Their high-leverage arms are leading the way: Trevor Megill (5 2/3 innings), Aaron Ashby (12 1/3 innings; more on his historic showing here) and DL Hall (5 1/3 innings) have combined for 23 1/3 scoreless innings this postseason with a .096 opponents’ average, and Abner Uribe had not allowed an earned run while appearing in each of the first six team games this postseason until allowing two runs (and giving up the lead) in the Brewers’ come-from-behind 6-2 win over the Dodgers in NLCS Game 3. He didn’t pitch in Game 4, so he will be particularly well-rested.
Any injuries of note?
Brewers: The biggest question mark for the Brewers is right-hander Brandon Woodruff, who spent the past two weeks making a last-ditch effort to make the World Series roster. After throwing off the mound prior to the NLDS for the first time since abruptly scuttling plans for season-ending shoulder surgery in August, Woodruff threw 31 more pitches off a mound in the visitors’ bullpen at Dodger Stadium during a workout between NLCS Games 2 and 3.
“I’m not really holding back,” Woodruff said that day. “I’m going as hard as my body will let me right now, because that’s where we’re at. I’m doing it in what I think is a good and safe way. I wouldn’t get on a mound if I didn’t think I could get on a mound. … I wouldn’t go do what I’m doing if I didn’t feel like I could do it.”
Who is hot and who is not?
Rays: Caminero officially joined the postseason party in Game 6 of the ALCS by slugging a two-run homer off the left-field pole against Cleveland closer Cade Smith. Díaz hit .333 with four doubles, two homers, four RBIs and a 1.061 OPS in the ALCS, and he leads the league with six extra-base hits in the postseason. Palacios went 6-for-12 with a big two-run double in the ALCS, and Simpson once again established himself as the lineup’s speedy spark plug. Hicks, DeLuca, Walls and Mesa didn’t provide much at the plate in the ALCS, but their defense was invaluable.
Brewers: Bauers won NLCS MVP by driving in six runs (twice as many as any other player on either the Brewers or Dodgers in the series). His 12-pitch walk turned NLCS Game 2 in the Brewers’ favor, and his 11-pitch home run in NLCS Game 3 gave the Brewers the lead in the seventh inning. … Contreras is also having a great postseason, hitting .367 with five RBIs in eight games. … Chourio is hot and not, all at the same time. He has a team-best seven RBIs this postseason, but has hit just .171 (6-for-35). His leadoff home run off Blake Snell in Game 3 of the NLCS gave Chourio 18 career postseason RBIs, moving him past Andruw Jones for the most postseason RBIs before a player’s 23rd birthday.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• This will be the first World Series game at American Family Field, but not the first World Series game in Milwaukee. Both the 1957 Milwaukee Braves and 1982 Brewers played at County Stadium, which sat just to the west of where the Brewers play today. There’s a marker for County Stadium’s home plate on the concourse of the youth baseball and softball field on the site today.
• Teams to score first are 23-12 (.657) this postseason going into the World Series, but Milwaukee has bucked that trend this October, going 5-1 when conceding the first run. All other teams are a combined 7-22 going into Friday night.
• It’s been 44 years since the World Series came to Milwaukee, and that’s a big number in these parts. It was worn by Hank Aaron, the former Milwaukee Braves and Brewers star who hit his 755th and final Major League home run at County Stadium 50 years ago this year.
• The Rays are 92-0 this year, including the regular season and postseason, when leading after eight innings. The last team to go a full year, including the playoffs, with a perfect winning percentage and at least 92 wins in those situations was the 2002 A’s (93-0). The A's, however, fell in the Division Series to the Twins.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] World Series Preview: Who are the Brewers?
item.dc:creator: Danny Russell
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays — the top team in the American League — has held its own to achieve the third pennant in franchise history, and their second this decade. The Milwaukee Brewers are back in the World Series for the first time since 1982, and they're doing it as the National League's best team. The 103-win Crew swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and now host the Tampa Bay Rays in a matchup of two franchise-first title seekers. Game 1 is Friday at American Family Field. Here's a position-b
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays — the top team in the American League — has held its own to achieve the third pennant in franchise history, and their second this decade.
The Milwaukee Brewers are back in the World Series for the first time since 1982, and they're doing it as the National League's best team. The 103-win Crew swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and now host the Tampa Bay Rays in a matchup of two franchise-first title seekers. Game 1 is Friday at American Family Field.
Here's a position-by-position look at the Brewers as they prepare for the Rays.
Catcher
William Contreras is the lead backstop for Milwaukee, and one of the most popular Brewers, as he has been one of the more reliable all-around catchers in the National League in recent years and in the playoffs, as his bat has stayed productive into October. He posted a strong 1.157 OPS with three homers through the NLCS while handling a staff that mixes elite velocity with a deep lefty presence.
At backup, the more familiar Gary Sánchez provides a power-oriented option off the bench.
Infield
The Brewers' infield blends elite defense, speed, and opportunistic offense.
- First base: Jake Bauers. The NLCS MVP has been the postseason story for Milwaukee. A well-known Rays prospect if you've read this site for any length of time, Bauers nearly retired but returned for what he considered one more season last year to keep his health insurance benefits after his wife became pregnant with their second child. Fast forward two seasons, and he has delivered lengthy at bats with power and timely hitting throughout October while providing solid enough defense at the corner. Veteran White Sox infielder Andrew Vaughn has also seen time at first and as a right-handed bat off the bench or at DH against lefties.
- Second base: Brice Turang. One of the best all-around second basemen in baseball and the No. 2 hitter. Turang combines Gold Glove-caliber defense with improved power (21 home runs and 100 RBIs in the regular season) and baserunning. He's a clear mismatch advantage and not to be trifled with.
- Shortstop: Cooper Pratt. The 22-year old rookie shortstop has started the bulk of the postseason games. He's shown a contact-oriented approach and improving glove work as the year has progressed, and pushing the previous starter Ortiz into a third base platoon.
- Third base: Joey Ortiz / David Hamilton. This has been a platoon/mix-and-match spot. The right handed hitting Ortiz and left handed hitting Hamilton now split time depending on matchups. If we are drawing comparisons, neither matches Junior Caminero's power, but both offer speed and defensive flexibility that fits Milwaukee's style.
Outfield
Milwaukee's outfield is built on athleticism, defense, and a rising star.
- Left field: Jackson Chourio. This 22-year-old superstar has continued his rapid ascent in 2026. Already with multiple 20-20 seasons under his belt, Chourio brings power, speed, and improving defense. He's the dynamic centerpiece of the lineup, their version of a Junior Caminero, and fun to watch.
- Center field: Garrett Mitchell. Strong defensive center fielder who has delivered several big hits in the playoffs, including a go-ahead home run in the NLCS clincher. He gets on base and covers ground.
- Right field: Sal Frelick. Elite defender with speed and contact skills. Luis Lara has spelled him against left-handers and provides another athletic option. The group ranks among the best defensive outfields in the league.
Technically also an outfielder, the Designated Hitter, Christian Yelich, remains in the lineup and was recently named club captain. While not at his peak production levels, his experience and ability to still impact games remain valuable, especially against right-handed pitching.
Rotation
Manager Pat Murphy has utilized short leashes and heavy bullpen support, but has a solid rotation heading into the World Series:
- Jacob Misiorowski — The clear ace and yet to be crowned NL Cy Young winner (16-5, 1.80 ERA, 252 strikeouts in the regular season). He's started Game 1 of both the NLDS and NLCS and will surely open the World Series. To say his high-velocity stuff that ranks among the best is an understatement. I half expected Misiorowski to mean fast in Polish, but apparently it's something closer to bear.
- Logan Henderson — The reliable No. 2. Solid second-half performer who has handled Game 2 duties effectively in his sophomore season as a homegrown talent.
- Robert Gasser — Emerged as the preferred Game 3 option after strong late-season form and solid postseason outings (including shutout work in the NLCS). He was acquired in the Josh Hader trade with San Diego, over came a UCL surgery in 2025, and started the year in Triple-A, making his rise a bit unexpected. His dad's best friend is evidently Vin Diesel.
- Dustin May (with Shane Drohan as an Opener) — May has postseason experience but has been used carefully; Florida State alumni Drohan opened Game 4 in the NLCS, and the southpaw seems likely to get the nod again given how well that went last time.
No starter has gone particularly deep in October, which is by design. Milwaukee trusts its relievers to take over after four or five innings, limiting any time-through-the-order penalties.
Bullpen
This unit has been the difference-maker. The Brewers' bullpen allowed just six earned runs across more than 40 postseason innings heading into the World Series and featured relievers earning the win in all four NLCS games during the sweep of Los Angeles.
- Trevor Megill — 6'8" Closer. Reliable late-inning presence, and a bit of an invention by the Brewers, having been added for a PTBNL in April 2023.
- Abner Uribe — Primary setup man. High-velocity right-hander who has been outstanding, despite blowing a save in Game 3 of the NLCS he's been their best bullpen arm this month.
- Aaron Ashby — Left-handed workhorse who has been nearly unhittable in October (multiple scoreless multi-inning outings) and got the save in Game 4 of the sweep.
- DL Hall / JoJo Romero — Additional lefty depth options that each were credited wins in the NLCS.
Regular season starter Kyle Harrison will likely find his way into the mix as well. The group throws exceptionally hard on average and enters the series fully rested after the NLCS sweep and the Rays' longer ALCS.
Conclusion
The Brewers' formula is clear: elite defense, contact and speed on offense, an electric frontline starter, and a lights-out bullpen that can cover the middle and late innings.
Against a similarly constructed Rays team that also emphasizes pitching, defense, and small-ball elements, the series should be tight, low-scoring, and decided by the margins. Milwaukee holds home-field advantage and the deeper, harder-throwing relief corps—two factors that could prove decisive in a first-time-champion showdown.

item.content:encoded:
Tampa Bay Rays superstar Junior Caminero is making baseball fun again, but Colin Cowherd is the fun police.
Caminero had his moment Monday night, hitting a monster seventh-inning home run off Cleveland Guardians closer Cade Smith that all but punched Tampa’s ticket to the World Series. The towering blast gave the Rays a 5-1 lead, and they won Game 6 of the ALCS 7-3 to advance to their third World Series in franchise history.
Perhaps more notable than the homer, however, is that Caminero took 38 seconds to round the bases. Caminero stopped several times to pose and pound his chest in celebration because, well, it was the biggest hit of his career.
“I think baseball sometimes needs to lighten up, that is way over the top rounding first… I’m all for flexing, that was obnoxious.” – Colin Cowherd on Junior Caminero’s home run trot https://t.co/H73MRXtpg0
— Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) October 20, 2026
“I am for celebrating; I think baseball sometimes needs to lighten up,” Cowherd admitted. “That is way over the top rounding first. Baseball for years was like, ‘There’s a way to play the game,’ and everybody else had a different idea on the way to play the game. But right before he got to home plate, he stopped, I thought, ‘Oh, this is obnoxious.’ Two things can be true: I’m all for flexing; that was obnoxious. It’s his style. He’s a bit over the top, it felt obnoxious to me.”
Rip players for celebrating after hitting a solo home run that made the score 8-2 in an elimination game. Mock teams for wearing goggles and popping champagne every time they clinch something. If this happened in the first inning of a June game, Cowherd would have a point. But when a home run essentially sends your team to the World Series, let the player take 38 seconds to flex.

item.title: [PCMag] Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays Livestream: How to Watch This Week's World Series Game 1, Even for Free
item.dc:creator: Jason Cohen
item.description: The MLB World Series is finally here after several weeks of intense playoff action. The Brewers swept the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time in 44 years. The Rays beat out the Guardians in six games to win the American League pennant for just the third time. Whoever wins, this will be the franchise's first championship. Which team will come out on top? Here's how you can watch every World Series Game live, and even for free. What Time Is the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays
item.content:encoded:
The MLB World Series is finally here after several weeks of intense playoff action. The Brewers swept the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time in 44 years. The Rays beat out the Guardians in six games to win the American League pennant for just the third time. Whoever wins, this will be the franchise's first championship.
Which team will come out on top? Here's how you can watch every World Series Game live, and even for free.
What Time Is the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays Game?
Game 1 between the Rays and Brewers will take place on Friday, October 23 at 8:00 p.m. ET.
How to Watch the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays?
This year, the World Series will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One app. You can also watch it with a live TV or sports streaming subscription from DirecTV, Fubo, Hulu, Sling, Sportsnet+ (if you're in Canada), or YouTube TV.
How to Watch the Brewers vs. Rays for Free
If you don't want to subscribe to any of the above platforms, you may be able to sign up for a few free trials to gain access to the remaining games. Fox One and Hulu offer three-day trials, DirecTV and Fubo offer five days, and YouTube TV gives you 10 days for free.
2026 MLB World Series Game Schedule
MLB's expanded postseason means more teams on the playoff schedule. In the Wild Card round, the Braves beat the Phillies, the Padres beat the Cubs, the Yankees defeated the Red Sox, and the White Sox defeated the Astros. The winners advanced to the Division Series, where the Los Angeles Dodgers, Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays, and Cleveland Guardians beat their respective opponents.
For the Championship Series, the Brewers beat the Dodgers in four games to clinch the National League pennant. The Rays defeated the Guardians in six games to capture the American League pennant. Now, Milwaukee and Tampa Bay will face off in the best-of-seven World Series to begin on October 23. Who will get to raise the trophy?
World Series: Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays
- Game 1 on October 23 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 2 on October 24 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 3 on October 26 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 4 on October 27 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 5 on October 28 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 6 on October 30 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 7 on October 31 - Fox/Fox One*
*if necessary
How to Stream the 2026 MLB Playoffs
This year's MLB postseason is stretched across multiple networks and streaming services. All Wild Card Series games for the American League and National League were broadcast on NBC, NBCSN, and Peacock. ALDS and ALCS games were on TBS/TruTV and HBO Max, while NLDS and NLCS games were on Fox/FS1. For the World Series, all games will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One streaming service.
- DirecTV: DirecTV's MySports base pack costs $45 per month for the first six months to see every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, and TBS/TruTV.
- Fox One: Fox's own streaming app lets you watch the NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox and FS1 for $20 per month.
- Fubo: Fubo's Sports plan costs $45.99 for the first month to watch the Wild Card Series, NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox, FS1, and NBC/NBCSN.
- HBO Max: If you pay for the $18.49-per-month HBO Max Standard, you'll be able to watch the ALDS and ALCS games on TBS/TruTV.
- Hulu: For $90 per month, you can watch every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, TBS, and TruTV.
- Peacock: Instead of a live TV service, you'd need to pay $10.99 per month for Peacock Premium to see the Wild Card Series games.
- Sling: The $60.99-per-month Sling Orange & Blue bundle will let you watch the ALDS and ALCS on TBS/TruTV and the NLDS and NLCS on FS1. Day Passes are also available for Sling Orange, allowing you to watch games on TBS for up to seven days.
- Sportsnet+ (Canada only): The $30-per-month Standard tier lets you watch every postseason game.
- YouTube TV: Though the standard plan for YouTube TV costs $83 per month, you can actually now pay for the cheaper $65 Sports package to see all games on Fox, FS1, NBC/NBCSN, and TBS/TruTV.
Can I Watch Postseason Games on MLB.TV?
Are you already an MLB.TV subscriber? You can watch the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series games through MLB's own streaming service—but there's a catch. To watch on MLB.TV, you'll first need to authenticate through a participating pay TV provider. It's such a sticking point that it makes the entire question moot. If you already have a TV provider, then you wouldn't need to use a streaming service. If you don't already have an MLB.TV subscription, don't pay for one now.
How can I listen to the 2026 postseason?
You can also listen to the games via ESPN Radio.
Which Teams Are In the Playoffs?
Since MLB expanded its postseason picture in 2022, a total of 12 teams make the playoffs each year. That includes six teams per league, including the three division winners and three Wild Card teams.
- American League Division Winners: Tampa Bay Rays (1), Cleveland Guardians (2), Houston Astros (3)
- American League Wild Card: New York Yankees (4), Boston Red Sox (5), Chicago White Sox (6)
- National League Division Winners: Milwaukee Brewers (1), Los Angeles Dodgers (2), Atlanta Braves (3)
- National League Wild Card: Chicago Cubs (4), Philadelphia Phillies (5), San Diego Padres (6)
Upgrade Your Streaming Experience
If you decide to watch the MLB postseason, there's still time to get a big-screen television for viewing this beautiful game. Pro tip: Turn on your TV's motion-smoothing option for the best picture while watching sports. Just remember to turn it off before watching other TV shows and movies to avoid the awful "soap opera" effect.
About Our Expert
As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert.
I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week.
My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth.
My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work.
Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.content:encoded:
Juan Soto
had a short message for Freddy Peralta after the Tampa Bay Rays star won the 2026 American League Championship Series (ALCS) MVP award on Monday. The New York Mets outfielder shared two comments on his Instagram story as the Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 in Game 6 to reach the World Series. Soto’s words came after Peralta turned his season around following a trade from New York to Tampa Bay in August. The pitcher’s strong playoff run has now earned him one of baseball’s biggest postseason awards.
Juan Soto’s Instagram Messages Follow Freddy Peralta’s ALCS MVP Award
Soto shared two messages in Spanish on his Instagram story on Monday. One read, “Did I tell you so or what?” The second said, “the best in the classroom 🔥,” according to the English translations provided.
The comments came on the same day Peralta received the ALCS MVP award after helping Tampa Bay win the series against Cleveland. The Rays took the series 4-2 and claimed their third American League pennant. They last reached the World Series in 2020.
Peralta was once Soto’s teammate with the Mets. However, New York traded the right-handed pitcher to Tampa Bay on August 2 after a difficult first part of the season.
Soto had his own challenges in 2026. The five-time All-Star hit .275 with 27 home runs but missed several games because of a calf strain.
His brief messages put the focus on Peralta’s big achievement, which came after a major change in teams and a much stronger finish to the season.
How Freddy Peralta Turned His Season Around With the Tampa Bay Rays
Peralta struggled during his time with the Mets. He went 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA across 22 starts in New York. After joining Tampa Bay, he recorded a 3.25 ERA over his final 10 regular-season starts, giving the Rays a much stronger option on the mound.
His work against Cleveland in the ALCS was even better. Peralta finished with a 0.75 ERA, nine strikeouts and just one run allowed over 12 innings. He won twice and also made a short relief appearance during the series.
In Game 6 on Monday, Peralta allowed one run over 5 1/3 innings as Tampa Bay secured a 7-3 victory at Tropicana Field. His performance helped the Rays finish off the Guardians and book their place in the World Series.
After receiving the award, Peralta summed up his feelings in a few words.
“This is crazy,” he said, before thanking the people around him.
“I’m very happy to be here, to be part of this great group and this organization. Milwaukee is always going to be in my heart, but it’s time to compete.”
The Associated Press and MLB.com reported on Peralta’s reaction after the game. CBS Sports also reported his ALCS MVP win and his strong postseason performance.
Peralta spent his first eight seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers before moving to the Mets in January. New York then traded him to Tampa Bay in August. Now, he will face his former Milwaukee team in the World Series.
The matchup gives Peralta a chance to compete for a championship against the club where he began his major league career. For the Rays, his late-season improvement has helped carry them to baseball’s biggest stage.
