item.content:encoded:
Junior Caminero News: Finally goes deep in Game 6
Caminero went 2-for-3 with a walk, a two-run homer and an additional run scored in Game 6 of the ALCS versus Cleveland on Monday.
The 23-year-old extended Tampa Bay's lead to 5-1 with a two-run shot in the seventh inning, which was his first home of the postseason. Caminero entered the contest with a .636 OPS through eight playoff games, but his Game 6 performance boosted his slash line to .273/.351/.455 in 43 plate appearances. With the Rays now headed to the World Series, he may have found his power stroke just in time.

item.title: [abc7.com] Where 2026 ranks among best World Series matchups since 2000
item.dc:creator: David Schoenfield
item.description: This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played. The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS,
item.content:encoded:
This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played.
The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, are in the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982 and seek the first championship in franchise history, looking to put an exclamation point on their season after leading the majors with 103 wins.
The Tampa Bay Rays were a 1998 expansion franchise and reached the World Series in 2008 and 2020 (the shortened season during the COVID-19 pandemic) but are seeking their first title as well. Young power hitter Junior Caminero and unheralded staff ace Drew Rasmussen lead the way as the Rays look to finally cash in after making the playoffs six times in the past eight seasons.
The Brewers and Rays led their respective leagues in wins, always a bonus for those who want the best teams in the World Series. Of course, a lot of attention will be given to the small-market aspect of the matchup, as the cloud of the lockout looms in the offseason.
Let's rank all the World Series since 2000 to see where Brewers-Rays fits in. This ranking is based on hype, the quality of the teams and their star power heading into the World Series. It's not a ranking of the quality of the World Series itself, although we're going to include a grade on that for each matchup. Let's get to it.
The Yankees were back in the World Series for the sixth time in eight years, and the Marlins had rebuilt after their fire sale following their World Series title in 1997. Trust me when I say that nobody wanted the Yankees in the World Series yet again. And the Marlins were merely a 91-win wild-card team. Most notably, however, both teams had spoiled the ultimate World Series by knocking off the Cubs and Red Sox -- before either team had overcome its curse -- in Game 7s in the LCS.
Actual World Series: C. The Marlins won Game 4 in 12 innings, when Yankees manager Joe Torre inexplicably failed to use reliever Mariano Rivera, and then 23-year-old Josh Beckett tossed a five-hit shutout in Game 6.
In an all-wild-card series, the fifth-seeded Rangers had won 90 games and the sixth-seeded Diamondbacks won only 84, making this the lowest combined win total in World Series history (for full seasons). The Rangers were going for their first World Series title, so there was that, and there were some fun hitters -- Corey Seager, the red-hot Adolis Garcia (who had just driven in 15 runs in the ALCS) and Corbin Carroll -- but it was a soft matchup on paper.
Actual World Series: D-. The series turned on Seager's tying two-run homer off Paul Sewald in the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, which Garcia then won with a home run in the 11th. There wasn't a single lead change after that, and three of those games were blowouts.
This was the Cardinals team that got hot in September and clinched a wild-card spot on the final day of the season when the Braves blew a lead in the ninth inning and lost in extra innings. St. Louis certainly had star power with the likes of Albert Pujols, Lance Berkman and Matt Holliday but had won a World Series fairly recently (2006), and the Rangers had just been there the year before.
Actual World Series: A. The first two games were one-run games, including the Rangers pulling out a victory with two runs in the ninth. In Game 3, Pujols blasted a record-tying three home runs. Game 6 was the David Freese Game -- perhaps the single most exciting baseball game ever played. Game 7 was a bit of an anticlimactic 6-2 Cardinals win.
The second-lowest combined win total in World Series history featured two wild-card teams that won fewer than 90 games. The Royals were at least a good story -- in the playoffs for the first time since winning the World Series in 1985 -- and had gone 8-0 in the AL playoffs, including an epic win over the A's in the wild-card game. The Giants, however, had just won the World Series in 2010 and 2012, and this team didn't seem nearly as good as those two.
Actual World Series: B-. Five of the games were blowouts, but it did at least go seven. It'll be remembered for Madison Bumgarner's historic performance: a shutout in Game 5 (the last complete game shutout in World Series history) and then five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, getting Salvador Perez to pop out with the tying run on third to end it.
The Red Sox were only three years removed from breaking the Curse of the Bambino in 2004, so although they were still a star-laden team with David Ortiz, Manny Ramirez and scrappy rookie Dustin Pedroia, they were no longer as interesting. The Rockies were a fun story, winning 14 of their final 15 games, including beating the Padres in a tiebreaker, just to win a wild-card spot. Then they went 7-0 in the NL playoffs and had won 21 of 22 entering the World Series.
Actual World Series: F.A dud. Two of the games were one-run games, but this goes down as one of the least memorable World Series of all time, with a forgettable four-game sweep.
The Tigers were the story of the season. They had lost 119 games three years before and 91 just the previous year. With rookie starter Justin Verlander winning 17 games, they led the AL Central most of the season -- only to lose their final five games and squeak into the playoffs as a wild-card team. The Cardinals won a weak NL Central with only 83 wins -- although they at least had Pujols at his absolute peak (.331/.431/.671, 49 home runs). Both teams hadn't won a World Series in a couple of decades: 1982 for the Cardinals, 1984 for the Tigers. Plus, it did feature two of the original 16 franchises.
Actual World Series: F. The Cardinals won one game in the bottom of the eighth, but it was otherwise a blur of nothing, most characterized by several fielding miscues by Tigers pitchers. David Eckstein won MVP honors without hitting a home run and while driving in only four runs.
The Braves were back in the World Series for the first time since 1999 -- they had made 12 playoff appearances in the intervening years without making it to the Fall Classic. Still, this was the weakest of the Atlanta playoff teams of recent vintage, winning only 88 games and missing Ronald Acuña Jr. for the playoffs. The Astros, meanwhile, were back in the World Series for the third time in five years -- but the first time since the 2017 sign-stealing scandal had broken in November 2019. Let's just say not everyone wanted them there.
Actual World Series: D. This was a weird World Series. The Braves ended up going with two bullpen games (who remembers that Dylan Lee and Tucker Davidson started?) after Charlie Morton broke a leg in Game 1. Astros starters kept getting knocked out early (the only starter to go more than five innings for either team was Max Fried in the finale). Four of the games were blowouts.
The Giants were back after winning in 2010, and the Tigers were back for the first time since 2006, featuring Triple Crown winner Miguel Cabrera and a strong 1-2 punch in the rotation with Verlander and Max Scherzer. This was also the last World Series with that season's MVP winners until Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani in 2024, with Cabrera and Buster Posey.
Actual World Series: D-. A boring sweep. Pablo Sandoval did hit three home runs in Game 1, but there were two shutouts and chilly weather in Detroit made the final two games unbearable.
This one did feature the two best teams from the regular season (both won 97 games), the last time before this year that we had that happen in a full season. It was also a classic original-16 matchup, although we had seen this in 2004 -- plus, both teams had won recently (2007 for Boston, 2011 for St. Louis). These were veteran teams, with Ortiz leading the Red Sox and the Cardinals featuring four .300 hitters, plus Carlos Beltran, who hit .296 and led the team in home runs.
Actual World Series: C+. Ortiz was absolutely locked in, hitting .688/.760/1.188 with two home runs and eight walks. The Cardinals were so scared of him by Game 6 that they intentionally walked him three times -- with two of those helping lead to rallies and a 6-1 Red Sox victory in the final game.
This one could be No. 25 -- it was during the pandemic, after all, and it was played at a neutral site in a half-empty stadium for social distancing reasons. But it was a great matchup between the teams with the best records in each league, albeit over the shortened 60-game season. You had Mookie Betts and Clayton Kershaw and Randy Arozarena in the midst of one of the best postseasons ever, plus the small-market Rays trying to beat the big-market Dodgers.
Actual World Series: C+. Because teams were allowed an expanded roster of 28 players, it was a parade of relievers -- but there were some fun games, including a bonkers ending to Game 4 and then Rays manager Kevin Cash's controversial decision to remove Blake Snell in Game 6, which backfired in a big way.
Maybe this should rate higher. After all, at the time, the White Sox were trying to break a World Series drought going back to 1917 and the Astros, born in 1962, had never won. But the White Sox's drought never had the same nationwide interest as the ones for the Cubs or Red Sox (fair or not) and these weren't particularly interesting teams. The White Sox were very good -- they won 99 games -- but lacked star power, with Paul Konerko their biggest name (Frank Thomas was on the team that year but played only 34 games and was injured for the playoffs). The Astros had Yankees transplants Roger Clemens and Andy Pettitte, but their two longtime stars, Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, were at the end of their careers (Bagwell, in his final season, was relegated to DH and pinch-hitting duties).
Actual World Series: C. It's hard to give a sweep a decent grade, but all four games were exciting, including Scott Podsednik's walk-off home run in Game 2 (after not hitting a home run all season) and Geoff Blum's go-ahead home run in the 14th inning to win Game 3.
The Phillies were back in the World Series for the first time since 1993 -- and hadn't won since 1980. They featured a powerful offense with Chase Utley, Ryan Howard, Jimmy Rollins and Pat Burrell. The Rays were maybe the unlikeliest World Series team ever: In their 10 previous years of existence, they had not only never had a winning season but had lost at least 90 games in each one. They won 97 games that year behind rookie Evan Longoria and power-hitting first baseman Carlos Peña, with speedsters Carl Crawford and B.J. Upton in the outfield.
Actual World Series: D+. Three games were decided by one run, but it was a pretty uneventful World Series. The lasting memory is the cold and rain in Philly that forced the midgame postponement of Game 5, the only time that has happened in World Series history. The game was suspended in the sixth inning and resumed two days later.
A Subway Series -- the first since the Yankees and Brooklyn Dodgers met in 1956 -- was certainly fun for the Big Apple, but it was less fun for the rest of the country (it drew the worst TV ratings at the time). The Yankees were going for a third straight World Series and had officially become the Evil Empire by that point. To make it even worse, they weren't even that good that season, winning only 87 games. The Mets were back in the World Series for the first time since 1986. There was certainly plenty of star power all around with the likes of Derek Jeter, Roger Clemens and Mike Piazza.
Actual World Series: C+. It was a tight-fought five-game series with all games decided by two runs or fewer. The turning point was the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, when the Yankees tied it off Armando Benitez and went on to win in 12 innings. Game 2 featured the infamous Clemens-Piazza bat-throwing incident, and the Yankees won the clincher with two runs in the ninth off a tired Al Leiter.
I know, the Astros ... again. Boo. But this was an absolute powerhouse of a team with 106 wins and stars such asYordan Alvarez (1.019 OPS) and Verlander (18-4, 1.75 ERA), plus the old standbys Jose Altuve and Alex Bregman. The Phillies, meanwhile, snuck in as a wild-card team for their first playoff trip since 2011 but were an immensely entertaining team with Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber& Co., as well as a passionate fanbase cheering them on.
Actual World Series: C. The Phillies won 6-5 in Game 1 on J.T. Realmuto's home run in the 10th inning. They took a 2-1 series lead, but then their bats died. Astros pitchers tossed a combined no-hitter to even the series, and Houston won the final two games 3-2 and 4-1, with Alvarez's three-run blast in Game 6 the deciding blow.
The Brewers' drought is the big narrative here as they try to finally cash in after their past decade of success, but we're still getting the 103-win Brewers facing the 98-win Rays, the best combined win total in the World Series since the Astros and Dodgers in 2017. (Not to mention we get a first-time winner no matter the outcome.) The Brewers aren't your conventional powerhouse team -- relying on speed, defense, timely hitting and a dominant bullpen -- but they do have one of the biggest stars of the 2026 season in Jacob Misiorowski, plus a rising star in young Jackson Chourio. The Rays might lack big names, although Junior Caminero is just the second player with two 40-homer seasons by age 22, and like the Brewers, they're trying to finally win it all after years of success.
Actual World Series: To be determined.
The Royals proved their 2014 World Series appearance was no fluke, winning 95 games with a better team that included trade deadline additions Ben Zobrist and Johnny Cueto. The Mets won the NL East behind a young, powerful rotation that featured Matt Harvey, Noah Syndergaard and Jacob deGrom. It was a fun matchup of teams trying to avoid lengthy title droughts -- 30 years for the Royals, 29 for the Mets.
Actual World Series: C+. It went only five games, but the Royals won the opener in 14 innings, won Game 5 with a three-run eighth inning and then won the clincher in 12 innings -- after Mets manager Terry Collins' ill-fated decision to leave in Harvey to start the ninth with a 2-0 lead.
This was a super entertaining showdown at the time. The Giants had yet to win a World Series in San Francisco and featured Tim Lincecum ("The Freak," for his small stature and overpowering stuff) and two rookies named Posey and Bumgarner. The Rangers had never won a championship and featured AL MVP Josh Hamilton and veteran DH Vladimir Guerrero. Both teams had pulled off upsets in the LCS, with the Giants beating the Phillies and the Rangers beating the Yankees.
Actual World Series: D. Meh. The Giants won the opener in a blowout as the Rangers made four errors and then tossed shutouts in Games 2 (behind Matt Cain) and 4 (behind Bumgarner). You can test Giants fans by asking them who won World Series MVP honors that year. Answer: Edgar Renteria (he hit .412 with two home runs and six RBIs).
Remember, this happened before the sign-stealing scandal changed how we view this era of the Astros. They had won 107 games behind the pitching duo of Verlander and Gerrit Cole and four players who mashed 30-plus home runs (which didn't even include Alvarez, a rookie that year). The Nationals were a wild-card team that had overcome a 19-31 season start to win 93 games and featured a starting pitching trio of Scherzer, Stephen Strasburg and Patrick Corbin (and 20-year-old sensation Juan Soto, who hit 34 home runs).
Actual World Series: B-. It went seven games -- the road team would win all seven -- although five of the games weren't close. The best game was the last one: The Nationals went ahead 3-2 in the seventh inning on Anthony Rendon's home run and then Howie Kendrick's go-ahead home run just inside the right-field foul pole.
This matchup began with a lot of hype: Shohei Ohtani, coming off his all-time game in the NLCS in which he hit three home runs and struck out 10 batters as the starting pitcher, against Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who had hit .442 with six home runs through the first two rounds of the playoffs. The Dodgers were looking to become the first team with back-to-back titles since the 2000 Yankees and the first NL team since the 1976 Reds. The Blue Jays were back in the World Series for the first time since Joe Carter walked off the Phillies in 1993. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts stirred things up after the NLCS when he said during the postgame celebration, "Let's get four more wins and really ruin baseball" -- a reference to the criticism of the Dodgers' high payroll.
Actual World Series: A+. The Dodgers won Game 3 in 18 innings on Freddie Freeman's walk-off home run, which followed an unlikely four-inning relief performance from Will Klein, the last guy on the Dodgers' staff. The Dodgers went back to Toronto trailing 3-2 but won Game 6 behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto and a crazy game-ending double play.
Game 7 featured two future Hall of Famers starting in Ohtani and Max Scherzer, more on-the-edge-of-your-seat plays than any game in World Series history, Miguel Rojas' unlikely home run in the ninth to tie it, as well as Will Smith's go-ahead one in the 11th -- and finally, Yamamoto pitching in relief to close out the game by inducing a double play with two runners on to win it for the Dodgers. It wasn't quite the greatest World Series overall, but two all-time games made it a classic.
The Angels, who joined the majors in 1961, were making their first World Series appearance, while the Giants, in the Bay Area since 1958, were trying to win their first title since moving from New York. You had Barry Bonds at the height of his unstoppable powers -- and trying to erase his own postseason demons -- while the Angels had a loaded lineup (Troy Glaus, Tim Salmon, Garret Anderson), the Rally Monkey and those deafening ThunderStix (let us pray they never return).
Actual World Series: A. Bonds was a beast, hitting .471/.700/1.294 (yes, that's a 1.994 OPS), but it wasn't enough. This series featured four one-run games, including a wild 11-10 contest and the classic Game 6, when the Angels rallied late from a 5-0 deficit to win 6-5. Game 7 was a drab 4-1 contest (Bonds went a harmless 1-for-3).
The Yankees had missed the playoffs in 2008 for the first time since 1993, so they went out and signed free agents CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett to add to an already stacked roster that included Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Robinson Cano, Hideki Matsui, Jorge Posada and Johnny Damon. Whoa. Yes, they were still the Evil Empire. The Phillies, trying to defend their title, had traded for Cliff Lee and then signed Pedro Martinez in July to bolster their rotation.
Actual World Series: C. It could have been a classic battle, but there were no one-run games and Game 6 -- Martinez's final start of his career -- was over early. The crucial contest was Game 4, when the Yankees scored three runs in the ninth off Phillies closer Brad Lidge to win 7-4.
This one presented conflicting emotions. The Yankees were going for an unthinkable fourth straight title, but in the wake of 9/11, there was a "Win it for New York" angle that the Yankees had never encountered. The Diamondbacks, meanwhile, had the big, bad duo of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling. When asked on the eve of the World Series about the Yankees' mystique and aura, Schilling provided one of the great quips in World Series history: "Mystique and Aura? Those are dancers at a nightclub." The Diamondbacks were not going to be intimidated.
Actual World Series: A+. Four one-run games, including three of the most memorable World Series moments ever: Jeter's Mr. November home run to win Game 4, Scott Brosius' walk-off home run to win Game 5 and then Luis Gonzalez's bloop single to beat the invincible Mariano Rivera in Game 7.
Two of baseball's most historic franchises had never met in a World Series, creating the classic showdown with games in Fenway Park and Dodger Stadium. It doesn't get any better than that. The Red Sox were a 108-win powerhouse -- with AL MVP Mookie Betts leading the way, backed up by J.D. Martinez, who hit .330 with 43 home runs that season. Chris Sale and David Price headlined the rotation. The Dodgers actually had a bit of a down year with 92 wins, but they also weren't lacking in big names, with Manny Machado (a trade deadline acquisition), Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Cody Bellinger and Justin Turner, with Kershaw and rookie Walker Buehler on the pitching side.
Actual World Series: C-. A letdown. The first two games in Fenway were cold and windy. Game 3 was an 18-inning affair -- the longest in World Series history -- but was more of a slog than a game to remember. Game 4 was the best of the series as the Red Sox rallied with nine runs over the final three innings to win 9-6.
This series had it all: dominant teams (both won over 100 games), long World Series title droughts (never for the Astros, 1988 for the Dodgers) and superstars galore (Altuve, Verlander, Carlos Correa, Kershaw, Seager, Bellinger, Yu Darvish). We didn't know at the time that both franchises were just kicking off 100-win dynasties -- let alone what the Astros were doing behind the scenes -- but the anticipation level was off the charts for the first matchup of 100-win teams in the World Series since 1970.
Actual World Series: A-. Game 1, with a start-time temperature of 103 degrees at Dodger Stadium, was a Kershaw 11-strikeout gem. The Astros tied Game 2 in the ninth on Marwin Gonzalez's home run off Kenley Jansen (1.32 ERA that season), both teams scored twice in the 10th, the Astros scored twice in the 11th on George Springer's home run and held on for a 7-6 win. Game 4 featured a five-run rally in the ninth by the Dodgers to win. Game 5 was completely bananas, with the Astros finally winning 13-12 in 10 innings. Game 7 was a letdown though, as the Astros won a 5-1 snoozer in which they scored five runs off Darvish in the first two innings.
As mentioned, what's not to like? Aside from Ohtani and Judge each playing in their first World Series and trying to put a final stamp on their legacy-defining seasons, we hadJuan Soto and Mookie Betts, a suddenly rejuvenated Giancarlo Stanton and a hobbled Freddie Freeman (only raising the drama if he hit well), Gerrit Cole and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Aside from the history between the clubs, we had both clubs needing to rewrite their recent history: The Yankees, back in the World Series for the first time since 2009, and the Dodgers trying to add a more legitimate championship to the one they won in the COVID-shortened season.
Actual World Series:C+. The Judge-Ohtani showdown was a flop, as Judge hit .222 with one home run and Ohtani hit .105 without a home run or RBI. The series also went just five games, with the Dodgers winning the first three. The series did produce two forever moments, however: Freeman's walk-off, Kirk Gibson-esque grand slam in Game 1 and the Yankees' fifth-inning defensive meltdown in Game 5.
The Red Sox were coming off their never-done-before comeback from down 3-0 to beat the Yankees in the ALCS -- and still had to beat a 105-win Cardinals team that featured Pujols (.331, 46 home runs), Jim Edmonds (.301, 42 home runs) and Scott Rolen (.314, 34 home runs), plus in-season pickup Larry Walker, who had an OPS over 1.000 that year. The Red Sox had their own ridiculous lineup with Ortiz (.301, 41 home runs), Ramirez (.308, 43 home runs) and Damon (.304, 20 home runs) plus a rotation with Schilling and Martinez. It seems inevitable now that Boston was going to win, but that wasn't the case at the time, so the buildup was intense.
Actual World Series: D. Blah. I mean, Red Sox fans will rightfully call it the best World Series ever, but after a sloppy 11-9 Game 1 played in a drizzle at Fenway (the Red Sox won despite committing four errors), the Cardinals never led again.
The Cubs had not only not won since 1908, but they hadn't even been in a World Series since 1945. The Guardians, meanwhile, had the second-longest drought of the original 16 teams, without a title since 1948. That was enough right there to build up the anticipation, but this also rates high because it was two good teams -- Chicago won 104 games while Cleveland won 94. Cubs third baseman Kris Bryant won MVP honors that year and Cleveland was led by 18-game winner Corey Kluber (who would start three times) and young rising stars Francisco Lindor and Jose Ramirez.
Actual World Series: B. The first six games weren't anything too special, but Game 7 was one of the greatest in World Series history. Cleveland tied it on Rajai Davis' three-run homer in the bottom of the eighth, the Cubs scored twice in the 10th -- following a stress-filled rain delay -- and escaped with an 8-7, curse-ending win when Cleveland had to bat little-used Michael Martinez with its season on the line.
]

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Rays' Junior Caminero Has Signature October Moment in ALCS
item.dc:creator: Nick Ziegler; Unknown
item.description: Despite being down in the ALCS two games to one and on the road for two more, the Tampa Bay Rays found a way to come all the way back and win three straight to punch their ticket to the World Series. item.content:encoded:
Despite being down in the ALCS two games to one and on the road for two more, the Tampa Bay Rays found a way to come all the way back and win three straight to punch their ticket to the World Series.
For a majority of the year, it was the Rays who were the best team in the AL, but it really looked like the Cleveland Guardians were going to be able to give them some problems. However, the starting rotation for Tampa Bay was strong in this series, and the offense finally got going in the last couple of games.
Offense was at a premium in the first three games, and the Rays were unable to score more than three runs in a game. Unsurprisingly, this resulted in them being down in the series. However, the unit finally started to come alive a bit.
Over the next three games, Tampa Bay totaled 17 runs, with two seven-run performances. In the clinching win in Game 6, it was Junior Caminero who was able to have his October moment.
Caminero Has His October Moment
After going 0-for-4 in the pivotal Game 3, Caminero came into Game 4 a bit more relaxed and ready to showcase what he can do. In the 7-3 win, he went 1-for-5, but was able to get a double and an RBI to help contribute.
In Game 5, he was able to go 1-for-4, in what ended up being a 3-1 Rays victory. However, with a chance to go to the World Series on the line, Caminero had his best performance of the postseason and was finally able to hit his first home run in October.
With this game still being very much in reach for the Guardians in the seventh inning, trailing by a score of 3-1, it was Caminero who hit a two-run home run to get Tropicana Field rocking.
At just 23 years old, he is one of the best young stars in the game, and the emotion with which he went around the bases showcased how excited he was to deliver in a big spot.
For the Rays, their being able to make the World Series with Caminero not even being at his best right now is very encouraging. However, he is a player that does hit his home runs in bunches, and the hope will be that he can carry this momentum from the ALCS into the World Series.
Nick Ziegler is an alumnus of the Connecticut School of Broadcasting. He has been working in sports media covering the NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL for nearly a decade with various publications online. With his free time, Nick enjoys being at the Jersey Shore with his wife, daughter, and their golden retriever. You can follow him on X, formerly Twitter, @NickZiegler20. He can also be reached at via email at NickZiegler26@gmail.com

item.title: [woonsocketcall.com] Brewers-Rays will produce a first-time champion, and maybe the first all-indoor World Series
item.dc:creator: RONALD BLUM

item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will play a Suds vs. Sun World Series that will produce a first-time champion and likely baseball's first all-indoor championship.
The best-of-seven showdown between low-payroll pennant winners opens Friday night in Milwaukee. It'll be the first World Series between title-less teams since the Philadelphia Phillies defeated the Kansas City Royals in 1980 and just the second since 1910.
One city is known for the television sitcom “ Laverne & Shirley," the home of Harley-Davidson motorcycles, cheeseheads and breweries that have included Miller, Pabst and Schlitz. The other is a vacation destination featuring warm weather, beaches and art museums.
“They’re highly athletic but so are we. I’m excited to see two great teams that play the game a little differently than maybe it’s been played the last decade or so,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said after his team defeated Cleveland in six games for the AL pennant. “We’re going to use our speed. We’re going to bunt when it’s called for. We’ll try to get matchups and I can assure you they’re going to do the same.”
Just five of the current 30 teams have never won a title, with Colorado, San Diego and Seattle also ringless.
“The city is ready. I know that the fans are ready, and I know that we’ll be ready,” said Milwaukee's Jake Bauers, MVP of the four-game sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NL Championship Series.
Milwaukee's Jacob Misiorowski heads the pitchers with his 100 mph-plus heat, and each team features a dynamic 22-year-old anchoring the lineup: Jackson Chourio of the Brewers and Junior Caminero of the Rays. Tampa Bay's Freddy Peralta and Drew Rasmussen could pitch against their former team.
“I don’t know how the people, the fans are going to take it, but I’m happy to be go there,” said Peralta, the ALCS MVP. “I have a lot of people that I love over there, people that care about me and I’m happy to be there and be able to compete together and take a lot of pictures and videos."
The Brewers started as the expansion Seattle Pilots in 1969, then were bought by Bud Selig's group in bankruptcy court and moved to Milwaukee for the 1970 season. The team's only Series trip was a seven-game loss to St. Louis in the 1982 Suds Series, back when the Brewers were in the American League.
Tampa Bay launched as the expansion Devil Rays in 1998 and dropped the “Devil” ahead of the 2008 season. The team's two Series appearances ended with losses to Philadelphia in 2008 and the Dodgers in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season.
Best face each other for 6th time in wild-card era
This will be only the sixth time since the start of the wild-card era in 1995 that teams with the top records in each league meet in the World Series after Atlanta-Cleveland (1995), New York Yankees-Braves (1999), Boston-St. Louis (2013), Dodgers-Rays (2020) and Dodgers-Yankees (2024).
Two low-payroll teams in Series for first time in 35 years
Milwaukee had MLB’s 19th-highest payroll as of Aug. 31. Tampa Bay was 25th.
Not since 1991 had both pennant winners been among the bottom 50% in player spending. Minnesota was 15th among 26 teams when it beat Atlanta (19th) in seven games.
Matchup with a ceiling
Tampa Bay’s ballpark has a fixed roof and Milwaukee’s is retractable — it probably will be closed with game-time temperatures predicted to be in the upper 40s or low 50s.
When all World Series games were played at retractable-roof ballparks in 2020 (Texas) and 2023 (Texas and Arizona), there were three open-air games each year.
The roofs of both ballparks came into play this postseason.
In the ninth inning of Milwaukee’s 3-2 win over the Padres in Game 1 of their NL Division Series, San Diego’s Ty France hit a high drive that appeared it might be headed over the left-field wall for a go-ahead homer until it struck a cable on the retractable roof in Milwaukee.
Two nights later, Yankees rookie Spencer Jones hit a flyball off a catwalk at Tropicana Field that was caught by Rays right fielder Victor Mesa Jr. for an out in the second inning of New York’s 5-2 loss in Game 2 of their AL Division Series.
Common ties
Greg Vaughn, Willy Adames and Matt Garza are the most prominent players with lengthy stretches on both teams, and Bauers made his big league debut with the Rays in 2018.
Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold worked for the Rays for nine years before Milwaukee hired him as an assistant GM in October 2015.
One of baseball's great nicknames
Those 1982 Brewers were known as Harvey's Wallbangers, a nickname given by first baseman Cecil Cooper. The Brewers led the major leagues in home runs under manager Harvey Kuenn and had a roster with five future Hall of Famers: Robin Yount, Paul Molitor, Rollie Fingers, Ted Simmons and Don Sutton.
Haunted hotel?
Various players over the years have claimed The Pfister Hotel, where many teams stay in Milwaukee, is haunted. Opened in 1893, the hotel has Romanesque Revival architecture, and players have claimed to hear spooky noises and footsteps.
If there is a Game 7, it would be played in Milwaukee on Halloween night.
Boss Man
Milwaukee's Pat Murphy, winner of the last two NL Manager of the Year awards, has two tattoos referencing Bruce Springsteen: “No Retreat No Surrender” on his left forearm and “The Boss” on his back.
He first went to a Springsteen concert in 1980 when he was in college, then another when he was coaching at Notre Dame.
“He grew up a Catholic kid in New Jersey. I was a Catholic kid from upstate New York,” the 67-year-old Murphy said. “There’s just so much that resonates with me how he speaks about things.”
Ballpark histories
The 1982 Series was played at Milwaukee County Stadium, home of the Braves from 1953-65 before they moved to Atlanta, and then the Brewers from 1970-2000. This year's championship will be played at American Family Field. Known as Miller Park from 2001-20, the ballpark is adjacent to the County Stadium site. It was host of the 2002 All-Star Game, which ended in a 7-7, 11-inning tie after both teams ran out of pitchers.
Milwaukee's ballpark is known for its Racing Sausages in the middle of the sixth inning, with the Brat, Polish, Italian, Hot Dog and Chorizo competing. It also has the Uecker Seat in the last row of section 422 in the left-field upper deck — it includes a bronze statue of Bob Uecker, the beloved funny man who broadcast Brewers games for 54 seasons until his death last year.
Tampa Bay's home, Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, is on its third name. Known as the Florida Suncoast Dome from 1990-93 and the ThunderDome from 1993-96, the stadium got its current name about 18 months before the Rays' first game in 1998.
Its only prior World Series games were in 2008, when the Rays split the first two games against Philadelphia before the Phillies won three straight at home. Tampa Bay's other Series appearance was in 2020, when due to the coronavirus pandemic the entire series was played at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas.
The Trop reopened this season after repairs to damage caused by Hurricane Milton. The Rays plan to move to a new stadium across the bay in Tampa in 2029.
Jersey watch
Milwaukee went 29-13 in cream uniforms during the regular season, 17-7 in pinstripes, 27-12 in navy blue, 9-6 in City Connect outfits and 21-21 in light blue. During the postseason, the Brewers are 4-0 in cream and 3-1 in navy.
Tampa Bay was 36-19 in home white, 32-33 in road navy, 8-2 in road Columbia blue, 12-3 in Devil Rays throwback jerseys, 6-4 in City Connect and 3-3 in road gray. In the playoffs, the Rays are 2-1 in home white, 2-0 in Devil Rays throwbacks and 3-1 in road gray.
Mirror mirror
Milwaukee was 32 for 128 (.250) and had a .347 on-base percentage in its NLCS sweep of the Dodgers, the exact same numbers Los Angeles batters had in their NLCS sweep of the Brewers last year.

item.title: [fansided.com] How many teams have never won a World Series? Either Rays or Brewers will make history
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: For the third time in franchise history, the Tampa Bay Rays are headed to the World Series. Thanks to another brilliant outing from Freddy Peralta and more big hits from their big three, the Rays polished off the Cleveland Guardians in Game 6 of the ALCS on Monday night. Led by ex-Rays prospect and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, the Brewers swept the Dodgers en route to
item.content:encoded:
For the third time in franchise history, the Tampa Bay Rays are headed to the World Series. Thanks to another brilliant outing from Freddy Peralta and more big hits from their big three, the Rays polished off the Cleveland Guardians in Game 6 of the ALCS on Monday night.
Junior Caminero and the Rays will now take on Jacob Misiorowski, Brice Turang and the NL-winning Milwaukee Brewers in the Fall Classic. Led by ex-Rays prospect and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, the Brewers swept the Dodgers en route to capturing their first pennant since 1982.
As if that weren't intriguing enough, we’re guaranteed to see baseball history, as neither the Rays nor the Brewers have won the World Series — and they’re not alone.
Which teams have never won the World Series?
As of October 2026, the Rays and Brewers are among five teams that have never won the World Series:
| Team | World Series appearances |
|---|---|
| Colorado Rockies | 2007 |
| Milwaukee Brewers | 1982, 2026 |
| San Diego Padres | 1984, 1998 |
| Seattle Mariners | N/A |
| Tampa Bay Rays | 2008, 2020, 2026 |
Unsurprisingly, all five franchises are expansion teams, with the Brewers (then the Seattle Pilots) and Padres debuting in 1969. The Mariners followed in 1977, and the Rockies (1993) and Rays (1998) joined in the two most recent expansions.
Who would have guessed the Rays, a franchise that didn’t have a winning record in its first 10 seasons of existence, would own three pennants since the start of 2008? Oh, and they’ve reached the World Series more times in that span than the Yankees, Blue Jays and Orioles. (That sound you hear is Yankees fans removing the chainsaws from their Halloween decorations and finding a new target to scare.)
As we discussed last week, the Brewers could become the second team to win the World Series after switching leagues. The Astros, who spent nearly five decades in the NL, achieved the feat in 2017 and 2022.
Milwaukee’s NLCS victory also means that all 15 National League teams have won a pennant while in the NL.
How did the Brewers and Rays do in their previous World Series appearances?
Well, they lost.
Jokes aside, we’ll head down Memory Lane and start with the 1982 Brewers. Led by Robin Yount and Pete Vuckovich, who respectively won the AL’s MVP and Cy Young Awards, the Brew Crew defeated the then-California Angels in the ALCS to capture their first pennant.
Milwaukee looked destined for a championship parade when the Brewers took a 3-2 World Series lead over the Cardinals. But the shift to St. Louis helped World Series MVP Darrell Porter and the Redbirds bring home their first title since 1967.
Yount was one of five future Hall of Famers on that Brewers team, joining Paul Molitor, Ted Simmons, Don Sutton and Rollie Fingers.
As for the Rays, there’s not much to say about their first World Series appearance. Chase Utley and the Phillies handled them with relative ease in 2008, and the greatest issue that October was the weather. If you’ve never experienced late-October rain in the Northeast, consider yourselves lucky.
The 2020 World Series was both forgettable and immensely more memorable, which is quite the contradiction. But the less said about 2020 as a whole, the better. Randy Arozarena’s postseason breakout is really the only thing that we personally remember.
Sorry, Rays fans. For your sake, we hope this year’s Fall Classic isn’t lost to time, too.
Evaluating the Rockies, Padres, and Mariners’ 2027 World Series chances
Forget whatever the way-too-early odds or prediction markets tell you … except as it relates to the Rockies’ World Series chances. You can effectively pencil them in for yet another losing record in 2027, regardless of how many games they play amid a potentially shortened season.
As we’ve discussed, speculation is growing that the Padres will make significant roster changes — including potentially trading likely future Hall of Fame third baseman Manny Machado — following an ownership change. Superstar outfielder/second baseman Fernando Tatis Jr. is likely safe, as is veteran shortstop Xander Bogaerts.
The Padres’ new ownership group recently emailed fans, saying the team is “all-in” ahead of the 2027 season. What that means, and whether it matters, depends on whether you’re an optimist or a pessimist.
We mentioned Arozarena earlier, and he’s a pending free agent who isn’t expected to re-sign with the Mariners. Seattle still hasn’t replaced Dan Wilson, and the organization overall reeks of dysfunction. If that sounds harsh, look no further than Cal Raleigh’s lack of leadership and the Mariners forcing Wilson to announce his own firing.
That said, the Padres have the best chance of these three to reach the 2027 World Series, though that’s not saying much.

item.title: [fansided.com] Rays and Brewers set for World Series showdown in updated MLB playoff bracket
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers
item.description: Just days ago, the Tampa Bay Rays were trailing the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS two games to one. Three straight wins later, they're back in the World Series for the second time in seven years and the third time in franchise history. Which means that now, our 2026 Fall Classic is officially set. And while it might not be the big-market showdown of Rob Manfred's dreams, it should be absolutely box-office baseball, as the two best teams of this season square off to try and make franchise histo
item.content:encoded:
Just days ago, the Tampa Bay Rays were trailing the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS two games to one. Three straight wins later, they're back in the World Series for the second time in seven years and the third time in franchise history.
Which means that now, our 2026 Fall Classic is officially set. And while it might not be the big-market showdown of Rob Manfred's dreams, it should be absolutely box-office baseball, as the two best teams of this season square off to try and make franchise history. Let's dive in.
Updated MLB playoff bracket after Rays advance to the World Series
And then there were two. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the World Series seemingly eons ago, dispatching of the Los Angeles Dodgers in a shocking sweep. Now that the Rays have knocked off the Guardians in the ALCS, our World Series matchup is set.
- World Series: Tampa Bay Rays (AL champs) vs. Milwaukee Brewers (NL champs)
It's not all that often that the top seed in each league meets in the Fall Classic; baseball's postseason is notoriously unpredictable. But these teams won 98 and 103 games in the regular season, respectively, and led the AL and NL more or less wire-to-wire. They were the best in baseball, and they proved as much in October. Now it's time to see which will make history and capture their franchise's first-ever World Series title.
Full World Series schedule: Milwaukee will be rocking for Game 1
We'll have a few days of waiting: Game 1 is set for Friday, Oct. 23, with first pitch from American Family Field in Milwaukee at 8 p.m. ET. The series will follow the traditional 2-3-2 format, with days off for travel after Games 2 and 5. Games 1, 2, 6 and 7 will be in Milwaukee, with Games 3-5 in Tampa.
| Game | Location | Date | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Game 1 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 23 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 2 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 24 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 3 | Tropicana Field | Monday, Oct. 26 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 4 | Tropicana Field | Tuesday, Oct. 27 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 5 | Tropicana Field | Wednesday, Oct. 28 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 6 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 30 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 7 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 31 | 8 p.m. ET |
The Rays are grateful for the break, as it will allow them to reset their pitching staff and line ace Drew Rasmussen up to face off against Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1. Clinching on Monday also allows Freddy Peralta to potentially get the ball in Game 2 on Saturday on full rest, with Nick Martinez likely behind him in Game 3.
Of course, the last thing the Brewers need is more rest. They clinched the NLCS in Game 4 last Thursday, Oct. 15, meaning they've already been at home for four days. By the time Game 1 of the World Series rolls around, it'll have been over a week since they last played a competitive game. Rust is overblown this time of year, but it's still something to monitor.
How to watch the 2026 World Series
This year's World Series will be broadcast exclusively on FOX.
- Dates: Oct. 23-Oct. 31
- TV channel: FOX
- Streaming: FOX One, YouTube TV, Hulu + Live Sports
You can also stream all the action on FOX One, provided you have a Fox One subscription ($19.99/month) or a valid cable login. You can also stream FOX through a variety of platforms, from YouTube TV to Hulu to Sling TV — all of which have free trials for new customers.
Pitching and power will define Brewers-Rays matchup
Suffice to say that runs are going to be at a premium in this series. Milwaukee ranked second in baseball in team ERA during the regular season, while the Rays were seventh. With Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and the best bullpen in baseball on one side and Rasmussen, Peralta, Martinez and All-Star closer Bryan Baker on the other, these teams have arms for days.
As such, it's going to be awfully hard to string together rallies — which means the team that finds a way to access some power will be at a distinct advantage. Neither team played much long ball during the regular season; both ranked in the bottom third of the league in homers, and neither ranked in the top 10 in slugging percentage. But the Brewers actually outslugged the big, bad Dodgers in the NLCS, and the Rays pulled away from Cleveland when their big bats (Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda) finally found the power stroke.
There won't be a ton of homers in this series. But whichever team has the most will almost certainly be hoisting the Commissioner's Trophy when all is said and done. If you're trying to play small ball against Abner Uribe, good luck.

item.dc:creator: Jason Cohen
item.description: As summer comes to a close and the air turns crisp, you know what's coming: the MLB Playoffs. The NFL season is already underway, and if you're also a baseball lover, this next month is essential viewing. The MLB has been through a number of changes in recent years. The Brewers swept the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time
item.content:encoded:
As summer comes to a close and the air turns crisp, you know what's coming: the MLB Playoffs. The NFL season is already underway, and if you're also a baseball lover, this next month is essential viewing. The MLB has been through a number of changes in recent years. From the universal DH and the pitch clock to video replay and an automated strike zone, baseball may look very different if you haven't been paying attention.
The Brewers swept the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time in 44 years. Now, it comes down to the Rays and Guardians in the best-of-seven Championship series. Which team will come out on top? Here's how you can watch live.
What Time Is the Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays Game?
Tonight's game between the Rays and Guardians will take place on Monday, October 19 at 8:08 p.m. ET.
How to Watch the Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays?
This year, the American League Division Series games will be broadcast on TBS. You can also watch them with a live TV or sports streaming subscription from DirecTV, Fubo, HBO Max, Hulu, Sling, Sportsnet+ (if you're in Canada), or YouTube TV. The World Series will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One app.
How to Watch the Guardians vs. Rays for Free
If you don't want to subscribe to any of the above platforms, you may be able to sign up for a few free trials to gain access to the remaining games. Fox One and Hulu offer three-day trials, DirecTV and Fubo offer five days, and YouTube TV gives you 10 days for free.
2026 MLB Playoffs Game Schedule
MLB's expanded postseason means more teams on the playoff schedule. Things started off with the best-of-three Wild Card Series, where the Braves, Padres, White Sox, and Yankees advanced. The best-of-five Division Series put them up against the Los Angeles Dodgers, Milwaukee Brewers, Cleveland Guardians, and Tampa Bay Rays, respectively. All of whom managed to advance.
The Brewers beat the Dodgers in four games. Now, it comes down to the Rays and Guardians in the best-of-seven Championship Series to determine the best team in the American League. The winner will meet Milwaukee in the best-of-seven World Series to begin on October 23. Who will make it all the way?
Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays - TBR lead 3-2
- Game 6 on October 19 @ 5 p.m. ET - TBS/HBO Max
- Game 7 on October 20 @ 8 p.m. ET - TBS/HBO Max*
*if necessary
World Series: Milwaukee Brewers vs. TBD
- Game 1 on October 23 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 2 on October 24 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 3 on October 26 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 4 on October 27 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 5 on October 28 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 6 on October 30 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 7 on October 31 - Fox/Fox One*
*if necessary
How to Stream the 2026 MLB Playoffs
This year's MLB postseason is stretched across multiple networks and streaming services. All Wild Card Series games for the American League and National League were broadcast on NBC, NBCSN, and Peacock. Additional rounds will be on other networks. ALDS and ALCS games are on TBS/TruTV and HBO Max, while NLDS and NLCS games were on Fox/FS1. For the World Series, all games will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One streaming service.
- DirecTV: DirecTV's MySports base pack costs $45 per month for the first six months to see every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, and TBS/TruTV.
- Fox One: Fox's own streaming app lets you watch the NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox and FS1 for $20 per month.
- Fubo: Fubo's Sports plan costs $45.99 for the first month to watch the Wild Card Series, NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox, FS1, and NBC/NBCSN.
- HBO Max: If you pay for the $18.49-per-month HBO Max Standard, you'll be able to watch the ALDS and ALCS games on TBS/TruTV.
- Hulu: For $90 per month, you can watch every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, TBS, and TruTV.
- Peacock: Instead of a live TV service, you'd need to pay $10.99 per month for Peacock Premium to see the Wild Card Series games.
- Sling: The $60.99-per-month Sling Orange & Blue bundle will let you watch the ALDS and ALCS on TBS/TruTV and the NLDS and NLCS on FS1. Day Passes are also available for Sling Orange, allowing you to watch games on TBS for up to seven days.
- Sportsnet+ (Canada only): The $30-per-month Standard tier lets you watch every postseason game.
- YouTube TV: Though the standard plan for YouTube TV costs $83 per month, you can actually now pay for the cheaper $65 Sports package to see all games on Fox, FS1, NBC/NBCSN, and TBS/TruTV.
Can I Watch Postseason Games on MLB.TV?
Are you already an MLB.TV subscriber? You can watch the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series games through MLB's own streaming service—but there's a catch. To watch on MLB.TV, you'll first need to authenticate through a participating pay TV provider. It's such a sticking point that it makes the entire question moot. If you already have a TV provider, then you wouldn't need to use a streaming service. If you don't already have an MLB.TV subscription, don't pay for one now.
How can I listen to the 2026 postseason?
You can also listen to the games via ESPN Radio.
Which Teams Are In the Playoffs?
Since MLB expanded its postseason picture in 2022, a total of 12 teams make the playoffs each year. That includes six teams per league, including the three division winners and three Wild Card teams.
- American League Division Winners: Tampa Bay Rays (1), Cleveland Guardians (2), Houston Astros (3)
- American League Wild Card: New York Yankees (4), Boston Red Sox (5), Chicago White Sox (6)
- National League Division Winners: Milwaukee Brewers (1), Los Angeles Dodgers (2), Atlanta Braves (3)
- National League Wild Card: Chicago Cubs (4), Philadelphia Phillies (5), San Diego Padres (6)
Upgrade Your Streaming Experience
If you decide to watch the MLB postseason, there's still time to get a big-screen television for viewing this beautiful game. Pro tip: Turn on your TV's motion-smoothing option for the best picture while watching sports. Just remember to turn it off before watching other TV shows and movies to avoid the awful "soap opera" effect.
About Our Expert
As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert.
I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week.
My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth.
My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work.
Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: [Jays Journal] Alejandro Kirk’s Blue Jays World Series run is inspiring AL East rival Jonathan Aranda
item.dc:creator: Matthew Sookram
item.description: Alejandro Kirk has always been one of the most likeable players in the Toronto Blue Jays clubhouse. His steady presence, team-first approach and easygoing personality have made him a trusted teammate. But Kirk’s “Mr. Nice Guy” influence isn't limited to the guys who wear the same uniform as him. With the pressure of the postsea
item.content:encoded:
Alejandro Kirk has always been one of the most likeable players in the Toronto Blue Jays clubhouse. His steady presence, team-first approach and easygoing personality have made him a trusted teammate. But Kirk’s “Mr. Nice Guy” influence isn't limited to the guys who wear the same uniform as him.
It has extended across the American League East, where Kirk’s longtime friend Jonathan Aranda is trying to help the Tampa Bay Rays capture their first World Series title.
With the pressure of the postseason mounting, Aranda turned to his childhood friend who had just lived through the grind of a pressure packed postseason. During the Blue Jays’ run to the 2025 World Series Kirk played in all 18 games and slashed .254/.349/.493 with a 132 wRC+ and five home runs.
“I was like, ‘Hey, do you have any tips for me moving forward here in October?’ And his main suggestion was, just have fun, just have fun and be yourself,” Aranda told Sportsnet’s Shi Davidi through interpreter Kevin Vera ahead of Game 5 of the ALCS. “That's honestly helped me a lot to kind of slow the game down and enjoy the moment and embrace this challenge of what is October baseball.”
That advice could not have come at a better time for the Rays' Aranda who went 0-for-10 through the first three games of the best-of-seven series against the Cleveland Guardians. Then in Game 4 he broke out with three hits, a walk, two RBI and two runs scored in the Rays’ 7-3 win.
Kirk’s advice allowed Arenda some time to reflect on the process how to revive himself and be the player everyone expected him to be. He encouraged Aranda to trust himself and remember why he was there. The 28-year-old first baseman hit 22 home runs during the regular season while slashing .274/.358/.434 with a 123 wRC+ and a13.8 offensive fWAR.
Longtime friends Alejandro Kirk and Jonathan Aranda have always supported each other
For Kirk, helping a player on a division rival didn't seem like a conflict considering the Blue Jays bowed out of the postseason before it even began. Aranda said the two “talk every day, we're best friends, we're brothers,” adding that Kirk is “someone that I have by my side.”
The support has always worked both ways. When the Blue Jays advanced to the World Series last year, Aranda flew in to support Kirk, saying “it was a big thing for me to go see him, for us, to see each other in the World Series.”
Watching Kirk make history on baseball’s biggest stage gave Aranda a chance to picture himself playing October baseball. He said, “In that moment last year, I kind of visualized myself in the same scenario. So now, fast-forward a year later, I use it as motivation right now. Hopefully I can make those dreams that I had last year a reality and help this team to a World Series berth.”
The Blue Jays would rather see their own players carrying Kirk’s lessons deep into October. Still, his role in Aranda’s run says something meaningful about Kirk’s off-field qualities that don't show up in the scorebox every day.

First pitch for the Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays game is set for 8 p.m. ET on Monday, October 19 at Tropicana Field.
The Rays lead 3-2 in the American League Championship Series after defeating the Guardians 3-1 in Game 5 on Sunday. Tampa Bay can clinch a World Series berth with another win, while the Guardians need a road victory to force a decisive Game 7.
Freddy Peralta takes the mound for the Rays after delivering 6.0 scoreless innings against Cleveland in Game 2. The Guardians, meanwhile, face a challenging pitching situation after using their bullpen for 7.0 innings in Sunday's loss.
Below, we'll break down our Guardians vs. Rays prediction and picks for Monday's ALCS Game 6, including the winner and player picks for PrizePicks.

Guardians vs. Rays Prediction, Spread, Over/Under for ALCS Game 6 – Monday, October 19
Tampa Bay enters Game 6 as the home favorites against the Guardians, returning a 1.63x payout if they win outright.
Here are the full payouts for the Guardians vs. Rays game on PrizePicks.
Team Picks data is live at the time of writing and is subject to change.
Peralta (0.79 ERA since August 26) will take the ball for Tampa Bay after delivering one of his best postseason performances in Game 2. The right-hander allowed just 4 hits and 2 walks while striking out 6, relying heavily on his four-seam fastball to overwhelm the Guardians.
Peralta (4.37 season xFIP) has been excellent since joining the Rays, going 5-2 with a 3.25 ERA. He's carried that momentum into October, allowing just a run over 10.2 postseason innings while recording 9 strikeouts.
He's rediscovered some of his early-career velocity, touching 99 MPH with his fastball in his last start.
Shawn Armstrong (2.35 postseason ERA) will open for Cleveland, with the Guardians facing elimination. The right-hander has been outstanding this October, allowing just 2 hits, recording 6 strikeouts, and issuing no walks over 7.2 scoreless innings.
However, Monday will mark his third appearance in as many days after he threw 1.1 scoreless innings in Game 5 and another scoreless frame in Game 4.
Cleveland will need significant bullpen contributions today. Regular-season starters SP Tanner Bibee and SP Joey Cantillo can provide length, while RP Hunter Gaddis, RP Erik Sabrowski, RP Tim Herrin, and closer Cade Smith could all factor in during the later innings.
One thing to note: SP Gavin Williams is unavailable on short rest after throwing 5.0 innings in Game 3, leaving the Guardians without their preferred starter in a must-win situation.
Cleveland's pitching staff must contain a Tampa Bay offense that's scored 10 runs over its last two games. The Guardians' relievers have performed well, but asking Armstrong to open for a third consecutive day before handing the ball to multiple pitchers creates a difficult challenge.
Guardians vs. Rays Prediction on Winner for ALCS Game 6 – 10/19/26
Here are the key stats and trends behind our Guardians vs. Rays prediction on the winner for Monday's ALCS Game 6.
Unless otherwise noted, data used in this article is from FanGraphs, Baseball Savant, and MLB.com.
- I like Tampa Bay to close out this series at home, a place where they've had tremendous success. The Rays went 58-27-0 straight up at home this season; their 68.2% home win rate ranks second in baseball behind the Milwaukee Brewers.
- Postseason baseball comes down to pitching, and the Rays are in a much better position when it comes to that. Peralta's already shut down the Guardians once, while Cleveland will rely on a bunch of bullpen arms worked to the bone.
- Peralta has fared much better at home all season, pitching to the tune of a 3.77 FIP compared to a 4.86 mark away from home.
- The Rays' offense has also been better at home, owning a 108 wRC+ at the Trop compared to 100 wRC+ on the road.
- Cleveland's wRC+ drops from 100 at home to 94 in road outings.
- Tampa Bay also has a slight bullpen advantage, owning the best relief xFIP in the postseason (2.80).

item.title: [MLB.com] LIVE on TBS/HBO Max: Rays-Guardians ALCS Game 5
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Keegan Matheson; Adam Berry
item.description: Sunday’s 5:08 p.m. ET game at Progressive Field will determine which side flies to St. Petersburg for Game 6 on the doorstep of the World Series and which team is fighting for their postseason lives. The Brewers get to kick their feet up and wait on the National League side, but over here in the American League, the stakes couldn’t be higher. The Rays are riding a high coming off their 7-3 win in Game 4, but as we’ve seen just about every day in this series, momentum can turn on a dime. The Guar
item.content:encoded:
Sunday’s 5:08 p.m. ET game at Progressive Field will determine which side flies to St. Petersburg for Game 6 on the doorstep of the World Series and which team is fighting for their postseason lives. The Brewers get to kick their feet up and wait on the National League side, but over here in the American League, the stakes couldn’t be higher.
The Rays are riding a high coming off their 7-3 win in Game 4, but as we’ve seen just about every day in this series, momentum can turn on a dime. The Guardians still feel like they’re playing their best baseball, going back to their incredible comeback to beat the White Sox in the ALDS, and they have a shot to take a commanding series lead in front of their home crowd Sunday.
“We're great. We're right in it. We're even,” said Guardians manager Stephen Vogt. “Again, now, it's a three-game series. I'll put our guys up against any team in the world in a three-game series. Of course, we would have loved to have taken a 3-to-1 lead tonight, but it's not in the cards. We can't control that now. We just show up, ready to play a good Game 5, and have a happy flight to Tampa.”
Drew Rasmussen will get the start for the Rays, and he’ll face Parker Messick, a premier pitching matchup on the biggest stage. These teams are starting to get aggressive, too, with the Rays using Freddy Peralta out of the bullpen in Game 4 while still keeping him available for later in the series.
The biggest threat to the Guardians now is the Rays’ Big Three of Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda, all of whom had big games in Game 4. Caminero’s was especially important, coming off four strikeouts in Game 3, and Aranda looks locked in. If that group can get back to Tropicana Field with a lead, look out.
“That was one of the main objectives that we had here coming into Cleveland, just to force the series back home,” Aranda said through interpreter Kevin Vera. “We're one of the best teams in the league when we're playing back on our home field, so we're going to use the fanbase and we're going to use that energy to push us forward. Drew is one of the best pitchers in the league, so it gives us a lot of confidence.”
After rain earlier this weekend, the forecast for Sunday is thankfully clear once again. It will still cool down as the evening stretches on, but the Guardians are used to these cold days, and the Rays, who play their home games under the dome at Tropicana Field, have already proven they can play in any environment.
When is the game and how can I watch it?
Game 5 of the Guardians-Rays ALDS is underway at Progressive Field. The game is being broadcast on TBS and HBO Max.
Spanish-language game broadcasts will be available on UniMas for the ALCS, and Spanish-language radio broadcasts will be available on Univision’s TUDN Radio.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Guardians: Parker Messick, LHP
Key stats: 5 IP, 6 H, 3 R, 0 ER, 2 BB, 3 K, 1 HBP in Game 2 
Messick started Game 2 on Tuesday, which initially lined him up to take the ball in Game 6 on Monday. The postponement that moved Game 4 from Friday to Saturday also moved Game 5 to Sunday, which allowed Messick to start this game on normal rest. The rookie lefty will be making his fourth postseason start; he logged a 3.09 ERA with eight walks and 14 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings over his first three outings.
In a season where Messick emerged as an anchor in Cleveland’s rotation, this is among his biggest starts.
“To be able to take the ball in this game shows the confidence the team has in me,” Messick said. “Hopefully I'm able to go out there and do the job because I know how important it is going into opposing territory with a lead, one game away from heading to the World Series. I’m looking forward to the opportunity, and hopefully I do my best out there.”
Rays: Drew Rasmussen, RHP
Key stats: 14 IP, 2 R, 2 BB, 17 K in two postseason starts 
One benefit of the rainout? Rasmussen can start this game on five days’ rest, the way he made most of his starts during the regular season. The right-hander delivered a quality start in Tampa Bay’s Game 1 defeat, pitching into the seventh inning and ultimately allowing two runs while recording 18 outs. He was even better in Game 1 of the ALDS, when he struck out 10 while allowing just one hit over eight innings against the Yankees.
There’s nobody else the Rays would rather have on the mound with a chance to take the series lead before heading back home.
“It's still just baseball. I think that's led to a couple of successful outings up to this point,” Rasmussen said. “Just try and not make it anything bigger than what it actually is. It's you. It's preparation, and it's execution. Those are really the only things I'm concerned with.”
What are the starting lineups?
Guardians: Cleveland has kept a standard lineup this postseason, with the only change for Game 5 behind the plate. Though Austin Hedges had caught all but one of Messick’s starts this season and Patrick Bailey hadn’t caught him once, the Guardians wanted to get Bailey’s bat in the lineup as they attempt to take a 3-2 lead in the ALCS.
Rays: Tampa Bay slotted in Ryan Vilade in right field in place of Victor Mesa Jr. for a touch more right-handed punch against the left-handed Messick.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Rays: Tampa Bay used five relievers behind starter Nick Martinez in Game 4, including presumptive Game 6 starter Freddy Peralta, but lefty Ian Seymour was the only one who threw more than 16 pitches. So expect the Rays to have everyone available between Rasmussen and closer Bryan Baker, who has finished each of Tampa Bay’s five postseason wins. Lefty Cam Booser has been the top left-handed option, right-hander Kevin Kelly gets most of the toughest right-handed matchups and setup man Tyler Wells asserted himself well with his two-inning appearance in Game 3. It’s possible that Griffin Jax, who started Game 3, could be called upon if needed. 
Guardians: Cleveland did not use closer Cade Smith and primary setup men Hunter Gaddis and Erik Sabrowski in the Game 4 loss. All three figure to factor into Game 5 as the Guardians look to take control of this series. In an ideal world, Messick will get Cleveland through five innings, if not six, and bridge the game to that trio.
Any injuries of note?
Rays: None.
Guardians: None.
Who is hot and who is not?
Rays: Simpson has been a spark plug of late, contributing a key single during the three-run rally in the fourth inning of Game 2 and then accounting for all of the team’s offense with his two-run triple in the fourth inning of Game 3. And the Big Three atop the order finally joined the party in Game 4, going 6-for-14 with five RBIs after a combined 5-for-34 start to the series. Maybe Hicks (3-for-20 in the postseason) and Mesa (4-for-25 with 11 strikeouts) will be the next ones to get going.
Guardians: Bazzana went 3-for-4 with a home run in Game 4. DeLauter’s first-inning RBI single in Game 4 was his 10th hit of the playoffs. That's one shy of tying Rocchio (11 in 2024) for the most hits by a Cleveland rookie in a single postseason. Rocchio went 1-for-3 on Saturday and is 4-for-28 through nine postseason games.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• Bazzana recorded his first career postseason home run with a solo shot in the 7th inning on Saturday, becoming the first Australian-born player to homer in MLB postseason history.
• Ramírez walked in the sixth inning to extend his postseason on-base streak to 16 games, which ties Steven Kwan (Oct. 8, 2022-Oct. 19, 2024) for the longest in Cleveland postseason history.
• Mesa recorded his second outfield assist of the postseason in Game 4, throwing out DeLauter at second base in the 1st inning. He’s the fourth player in Rays postseason history with multiple outfield assists, joining B.J. Upton, Kevin Kiermaier and Hunter Renfroe (each had two outfield assists for the Rays).

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] Rays’ Aranda leaning on advice from Blue Jays’ Kirk during post-season
item.dc:creator: Shi Davidi
item.description: CLEVELAND – Jonathan Aranda and Alejandro Kirk are childhood friends, and before the post-season started, the Tampa Bay Rays first baseman reached out to the Toronto Blue Jays catcher for some advice. “I was like, ‘Hey, do you have any tips for me moving forward here in October?’ And his main suggestion was, just have fun, just have fun and be yourself,” Aranda said through interpreter Kevin Vera ahead of ALCS Game 5. “That's honestly helped me a lot to kind of slow the game down and enjoy the m
item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND – Jonathan Aranda and Alejandro Kirk are childhood friends, and before the post-season started, the Tampa Bay Rays first baseman reached out to the Toronto Blue Jays catcher for some advice.
“I was like, ‘Hey, do you have any tips for me moving forward here in October?’ And his main suggestion was, just have fun, just have fun and be yourself,” Aranda said through interpreter Kevin Vera ahead of ALCS Game 5. “That's honestly helped me a lot to kind of slow the game down and enjoy the moment and embrace this challenge of what is October baseball.”
Aranda went 0-for-10 through the first three games of the best-of-seven against the Cleveland Guardians before breaking out with three hits, a walk, two RBIs and two runs scored in Saturday's 7-3 win in Game 4.
He and Kirk “talk every day, we're best friends, we're brothers,” and added that “he’s someone that I have by my side.”
Last year, they both went to the all-star game together, but Aranda’s season was truncated by a fractured left wrist suffered July 31, a factor in the Rays falling out of playoff contention.
Still, when the Blue Jays advanced to the World Series, Aranda flew in to follow Kirk, saying “it was a big thing for me to go see him, for us, to see each other in the World Series.”
“In that moment last year, I kind of visualized myself in the same scenario,” he continued. “So now, fast-forward a year later, I use it as motivation right now. Hopefully I can make those dreams that I had last year a reality and help this team to a World Series berth.”

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Back-and-Forth ALCS Could Spell Trouble for Brewers in World Series
item.dc:creator: Curt Bishop
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers made quick work of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series to secure their first trip to the World Series in 44 years. Now, the Brewers are awaiting the winner of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays, which is tied at two games apiece heading into Sunday's Game 5. The series will go at least six games at this point, which means whoever wins it will only have a few days off before the series beg
item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers made quick work of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series to secure their first trip to the World Series in 44 years. Now, the Brewers are awaiting the winner of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays, which is tied at two games apiece heading into Sunday's Game 5.
The series will go at least six games at this point, which means whoever wins it will only have a few days off before the series begins. This could ultimately spell some trouble for the Brewers, who have a ton of extra rest.
How extra rest can affect teams
Extra rest can help. The Washington Nationals had a week over before the 2019 World Series while the Houston Astros only had two days. Washington proceeded to win the first two games on the road and ultimately win the series in seven games.
However, there have been plenty of cases in which extra rest hasn't exactly been kind to teams. The Detroit Tigers had a week off before the 2006 World Series, while the St. Louis Cardinals won the NLCS in seven games and only had one day. St. Louis made quick work of the Tigers, winning in five games.
The same thing happened to Detroit in 2012 when they swept the ALCS and waited around for the San Francisco Giants to come back from 3-1 to win the series. At that point, the Giants had the momentum and ultimately swept the Tigers.
The 2007 Colorado Rockies and 2015 New York Mets also had extra rest before the World Series and were eliminated quickly. So, it can certainly hurt at times.
Perhaps it could ultimately help the Brewers instead. There's really no way of knowing for sure, as it can work both ways. But things will get interesting if the ALCS goes the full seven games. The winner of that series would only have two days off before the series while Milwaukee will have had over a week.
A case could be made that it just gives the Brewers more time to prepare, and that is certainly true. But teams can also lose their edge when they aren't playing for a week or more before the World Series, so it will be very interesting to see just how it affects the Brewers as they prepare for their first World Series since 1982.
Curt Bishop is a freelance sports writer who graduated from Maryville University of St. Louis with a Bachelor of Arts degree in the field of Communication and currently writes as a contributor for various platforms covering Major League Baseball. Curt’s work includes covering trade and free agency predictions, as well as rumors and news.
